tool_name: AgentsLeak: Runtime Protection for AI Coding Agents
description: AgentsLeak is an open-source runtime security platform that hooks into AI coding agent engines (Claude Code, Cursor) and enforces security policies before every action. It monitors file access, network connections, process creation, and command execution with real-time blocking, behavioral sequence detection, and a security dashboard. Think endpoint protection, but purpose-built for AI agent sessions.

tool_name: AI Attack & Defence Wargame: The Insurance Company Edition
description:
A live, adversarial wargame where every participant controls an AI-powered insurance chatbot built on LLM and tries to break everyone else's.
Each bot ships with a domain-specific knowledge, and sensitive customer data including Tax File Numbers. Your job is to harden your bot against prompt injection, indirect instruction override, and data exfiltration while actively probing rival bots to extract what they're supposed to protect.
This is not a CTF with static flags. The attack surface evolves as defenders patch and attackers adapt. You read your own source code, identify the trust boundary failures, push a fix, and watch whether it holds under live adversarial pressure.

Right at the start, there will be a briefing to show how to play in the wargame. Knowledge of the OpenAI Python SDK helps but is not a requirement. Each player has access to their chatbot source code repository where they can run, test, debug and push their changes.

tool_name: ConfigManBearPig - Identify, Visualize, and Navigate SCCM Attack Paths in BloodHound
description: With only a low-privileged Active Directory domain context, ConfigManBearPig collects enough data from a Microsoft Configuration Manager (formerly SCCM) environment to identify all attack paths documented in the Misconfiguration Manager knowledgebase that allow complete TAKEOVER of SCCM hierarchies, as well as several ELEVATE (privilege escalation) and CRED (credential gathering) attack techniques, then maps and connects them to the BloodHound graph for interactive exploration and querying.

tool_name: Intercept.js: Context-Aware YARA for Runtime Detection In JavaScript Environments
description:
Many modern attacks unfold inside JavaScript runtimes — browsers, email clients, and Office add-ins — where traditional file-scanning and OS-level controls have limited visibility into application-layer context. In these environments, payloads may exist only as in-memory buffers, fetch responses, or dynamically generated objects. Effective detection requires consideration of not only what bytes exist, but also where they originated and how they are being used.

To address this visibility gap, we present Intercept.js, an open-source detection engine written in vanilla JavaScript that fuses byte-level pattern matching with runtime context inside a unified rule model.

While compatible with standard YARA syntax and modules (PE, ELF, Math, Hash, String, Time), Intercept.js extends detection beyond file scanning. Rules can combine content inspection with contextual metadata such as domain novelty, sender reputation, MIME discrepancies, user gesture state, and runtime origin. Its pluggable module architecture allows developers and security teams to inject custom contextual signals and expose them directly to rule authors, extending YARA from a file signature language into a runtime-aware decision engine.

This enables detections like:
- Executable header from a newly observed domain
- Macro-enabled document from an unknown sender
- Clipboard-inserted script without user interaction
- Binary content with MIME mismatch

Optimized for constrained environments using Aho-Corasick matching, RegExp acceleration, and enforced match caps, Intercept.js runs anywhere JavaScript runs. It enables security teams to shift detection left, disrupting attacker tooling at ingress (T1105), malicious paste events (T1204.004), phishing attachments (T1566.001), and client-side data exfiltration (T1048) — before payloads ever reach disk.

During Arsenal, we will demonstrate real-time clipboard defense by intercepting a ClickFix/FileFix-style attack within a browser extension, showing how content and context are evaluated together to detect malicious in-memory payloads. We will also discuss the engine's open plug-in interface and illustrate how it operates unchanged across webpages and serverless platforms.

tool_name: LLM Hacking 101
description:
Large Language Models are increasingly embedded into applications, automation platforms, and security tooling - yet their attack surface remains poorly understood. This 2-hour hands-on Arsenal lab introduces practical offensive techniques against LLM-powered and agentic systems.

Participants will progress from foundational jailbreak development to guardrail bypass techniques, exploring both direct and indirect prompt injection attacks. The lab will also introduce basic agent tool enumeration and exploitation, demonstrating how reasoning layers and tool integrations can be manipulated to extend attacker influence.

All exercises are delivered through a dedicated hands-on environment using the PwnBox.AI platform. Attendees will exploit realistic AI-enabled scenarios, chain techniques together, and gain practical experience identifying where traditional security assumptions break down in LLM-integrated systems.

tool_name: Obscurize: Malware for Defense and Counter Offense
description: What if we could use the creativity of threat actors against them? In this case, using a rootkit to develop a security tool which can be used defensively AND offensively. Malware the Securonix Threat Research team has dissected quite commonly enumerates its environment before detonating. It checks BIOS strings, MAC OUI prefixes, RAM amount, running services, and process lists to detect sandboxes and analyst VMs. If a VM is detected, the malware simply exits. STR has build a tool called Obscurize to fight fire with fire. By adapting the userland DLL injection techniques of the r77 rootkit found in OBSCURE#BAT, a publication by our research team, Obscurize deploys 20 Detours API hooks across every running process with zero kernel driver requirement. It has two modes - Defensive and Trap. Defensive mode makes real physical hardware present itself as a virtual machine spoofing checks malware is know to use to evade sandboxes. Trap mode inverts this making a VM appear to be genuine hardware so analysts can ensure their samples pass all their pre-execution checks. The architecture is a Windows Service that reflectively injects agent DLLs into every new process, reads live configuration from the registry, and exposes a named-pipe control interface. Spoofing is applied at the API layer including GetSystemFirmwareTable for raw SMBIOS data, NtQueryValueKey for registry BIOS keys, and stdout interception for systeminfo.exe. This approach ensures consistent results across both legacy Win32 and modern WMI/PowerShell query paths. Obscurize is currently privately published to Github and will be avaialble as an open source tool at the completion of its presentation and demonstration.

tool_name: Pentest Copilot V2: The Agentic Pentesting Workspace
description:
Pentest Copilot V2 is a AI-native unified browser based workspace for offensive security. It gives pentesters, red teamers, CTF solvers, and security researchers a single interface to launch and run workflows across reconnaissance, exploitation support, scripting, automation, web testing, and general assessment tasks. Instead of stitching together terminals, browser tabs, notes, proxies, and one-off scripts, users work from one environment designed to make offsec workflows faster, cleaner, and easier to manage.

V2 moves Pentest Copilot from a heavily human-in-the-loop assistant to a far more autonomous system. It can execute multi-step tasks with less operator babysitting, use parallel subagents, integrate with established security tooling, automate browser-driven workflows when useful, and apply guardrails for safer use in authorized environments. It is designed for real security work across pentests, red teaming, labs, and CTFs.

tool_name: ShadowHunt 2.0: Uncovering Shadow IT and Hidden Secrets
description:
ShadowHunt is a tool designed to expose one of the most dangerous blind spots in modern enterprise security: Shadow IT on Public Repositories.

In today's decentralized, developer-driven world, employees often use personal accounts (GitHub, Docker Hub, Helm Charts) to push company code, test infrastructure, or fork internal projects, without anyone knowing. ShadowHunt identifies and maps these personal repositories back to organizational employees by analyzing public repository activity (GitHub, Docker Hub, Quay, GIST, GCHR), commit metadata, manifests, templates and contributor patterns. Once linked, it scans those personal repos for leaked secrets - tokens, keys, and config files that quietly jeopardize your organization's security.

Beyond Shadow IT discovery, ShadowHunt also detects secrets that evade traditional scanners by generating base64 permutations and scanning public repositories for these hidden variants.

Whether you're defending your supply chain or hunting for bounty, ShadowHunt gives you visibility where it matters most—outside your perimeter.

tool_name: Social Engineering with Reel
description: Reel is a workflow-driven, flexible phishing framework supporting credential capture campaigns with optional real-time MFA relay, as well as email sending. All elements are fully configurable via a workflow system, allowing complex campaigns to be developed. A plugin system allows operators to extend Reel's core functionality without requiring code changes.

tool_name: Tengu Marauder Vanguard Version 2.0
description:
The Tengu Marauder Vanguard 2.0 is an open-source robotic cybersecurity platform designed for physical red team operations and assessing vulnerabilities in wireless networks. The platform utilizes the Raspberry Pi 5, enabling an operator to deploy and manage units throughout a designated environment from a single interface. This interface, developed on Flask, features a tailored framework. It offers real-time visualization of targets, integrated network scanning, and cohesive management of units.

Version 2.0 introduces significantly more features compared to the original Tengu Marauder. Protocol coverage encompasses Bluetooth scanning and SDR-based RF tools. The integration of an ESP32-C5 module introduces dual-band 2.4/5 GHz WiFi testing, enabling you to evaluate contemporary wireless environments that were once inaccessible. The Hailo AI HAT 2 and Fusion HAT+ work together to bring AI inference directly to the robot, allowing it to analyze targets and make decisions on its own without needing the cloud.

A Banana Pi BPI-R4 operating on OpenWrt manages network coordination among various units. It serves as the primary network controller for the platform, offering access point functionality, traffic routing, and reliable connectivity for all deployed units.

Tengu Marauder Vanguard 2.0 is designed for cyber operators with authorization, wireless security researchers, and individuals who assess physical and RF attack surfaces in corporate and IoT environments.

tool_name: ThreatShield - The Intelligent Way of Threat Modelling
description: ThreatShield is an AI-powered threat modeling and security analysis tool designed to automate and elevate threat modeling using OpenAI's enterprise API. It processes raw documents like PRDs, architecture diagrams, confluence docs, slack threads and meeting transcripts to generate structured STRIDE and PASTA based threat models, attack trees, DREAD scoring, mitigations and ASVS Test Cases.

tool_name: VulnZoo: A Complete Vulnerable IoT Ecosystem for Security Research and Training
description: VulnZoo is an open-source ecosystem of vulnerable devices designed to fill the gap in practical cybersecurity training in embedded, medical, industrial and automotive environments. Unlike current platforms that focus on isolated components, VulnZoo models a complete IoT product from device firmware to mobile applications and cloud services allowing the study of realistic attack chains between multiple components.

tool_name: Azazel-Edge : Deterministic Edge Decision Support for Constrained SOC/NOC Operations
description:
Azazel-Edge is a deterministic edge decision appliance for small, temporary, and rapidly deployed networks where defenders must act under constraint: limited infrastructure, limited personnel, unstable connectivity, and little time to decide. Its core contribution is an explicit and auditable local decision loop that evaluates operational reliability (NOC) and security threat context (SOC) separately, resolves them through a deterministic action arbiter, and records selected evidence, rejected alternatives, and structured explanation.

The live path is layered. Tactical Engine performs first-minute triage on time-sensitive security events. Evidence Plane and deterministic evaluators then add second-pass context across multiple local sources. Optional AI assistance is bounded to operator support such as explanation, triage guidance, and runbook-oriented review; it does not participate in the core action-selection mechanism.

Azazel-Edge targets environments where network availability is part of the mission and centralized infrastructure may be absent or impractical: disaster-response networks, emergency coordination sites, field operations, exercises, isolated internal networks, and rapidly assembled local deployments. For demonstration, it uses deterministic replay rather than opaque live-only telemetry so evaluator outputs, arbitration logic, and explanation remain stable and inspectable in a short Arsenal session. The replay path is for demonstration only and does not replace the live Tactical first-pass path used in normal operation.

tool_name: capa: Beyond Disassembly: Dynamic Matching for Static Blindspots
description:
Static analysis typically provides limited visibility into packed samples and overly complex or obfuscated modern binaries—such as large Rust and Go targets. While dynamic analysis runs the sample to bypass these static limitations, it generates detailed execution traces that can be difficult to triage manually. capa addresses this by applying its rule-based matching engine directly to dynamic execution data.

Attend this comprehensive demonstration to learn how capa enables consistent capability recovery across both static and dynamic domains. We will explore capa's dynamic matching engine, demonstrating how it groups and sequences related API calls to identify complex behaviors like memory allocation and code injection post-unpacking/de-obfuscation. See firsthand how this methodology allows analysts to identify high-level intent and automate response workflows even for the most complex binaries.

tool_name: Chef Special: Updates to CSTC - CyberChef-inspired Message Transformator in BurpSuite
description:
Imagine GCHQ's CyberChef integrated in BurpSuite, with live modification of requests at your fingertips. That's exactly what we had in mind when we built the Cyber Security Transformation Chef. CSTC is an extension to the popular BurpSuite Proxy built for experts working with web applications. It enables users to define recipes that are applied to outgoing or incoming HTTP requests/responses automatically. Whatever quirks and specialties an application might challenge you with during an assessment, the CSTC has you covered.
As an example, imagine an API that requires an HMAC appended to all messages derived from datapoints inside the message body. With the CSTC you can extract the necessary datapoints with ease and calculate the HMAC on the fly – automatically for all requests. Together with the CSTCs integration into all major BurpSuite components you can now perform automatic intrusion tests with the Scanner, or manual fuzzing using Intruder and Repeater, without worrying about the HMAC any longer. Another use case is to extract JWTs from incoming HTTP responses and use them in outgoing requests of the Scanner. This eliminates the need to worry about expiring JWTs while scanning.
After our last visit to the Arsenal in 2024 we're back! The CSTC contains new features and improvements, driven by [GM1.1]community feedback, such as many new operations to be used in recipes, enhanced capabilities for sending requests and handling conditionals. In addition, the new CSTC supports multiple active recipes in parallel. Overall, the latest changes make it even simpler to automate application-specific data structures to ensure a maximum focus for pentesters on what's most important: discovering vulnerabilities.

tool_name: Cleric: ETW Sandbox and Memory Scanner
description:
Cleric is an integrated Windows malware analysis framework designed for deep runtime inspection of suspicious processes. It combines four components into a unified pipeline:

1. Paladin: a C++ memory scanner performing 15 detection techniques across threads, memory regions, modules, and system call stubs, identifying indicators such as RWX regions, callstack anomalies, IAT/EAT hooks, syscall patching, and defensive API tampering.

2. Warlock: a C# orchestrator that coordinates scanning alongside PE-Sieve analysis, Frida API hooking (23+ Windows APIs), and real-time ETW/Sysmon event collection, packaging results into
portable archives.

3. Cleric: a Python ETL pipeline that ingests, normalises, and enriches scan data from all collectors, outputting to JSON, CSV, SQLite, or MongoDB.

4. A React + FastAPI dashboard that visualises detections, process timelines, network activity, and investigation graphs through a CRT-styled terminal interface.

Data flows from live Windows targets through the collection and enrichment pipeline into a queryable store, giving analysts a single-pane view of process-level behaviour, memory anomalies, API activity, and system events.

tool_name: findmytakeover - find dangling domains in a multi cloud environment
description: findmytakeover detects dangling DNS record in a multi cloud environment. It does this by scanning all the DNS zones and the infrastructure present within the configured cloud service provider either in a single account or multiple accounts and finding the DNS record for which the infrastructure behind it does not exist anymore rather than using wordlist or bruteforcing DNS servers.

tool_name: Ghostwriter
description:
Ghostwriter is a completely free and open-source platform designed to enhance offensive security operations by simplifying report writing, asset tracking, and assessment management. It offers tools for managing clients, creating a reusable findings library, and organizing the infrastructure and domains utilized during assessments. With its powerful reporting engine, Ghostwriter includes comprehensive collaborative writing features and customizable report templates, allowing teams to produce polished deliverables with minimal manual effort.

Ghostwriter has grown significantly since it debuted at Black Hat Arsenal in 2019. Today, we're excited to showcase developments from the past year of releases, including fully Google Docs-style collaborative report editing, collaborative project notes, and integration with BloodHound Community Edition for reporting.

tool_name: Hecate: a trivial UART tool
description:
Hecate (https://tigard-tools/hecate) is an open-source embedded UART implant development framework designed to make common hardware hacking tasks fast, flexible, and achievable with minimal code. It turns any CircuitPython-compatible microcontroller into a powerful, customizable UART implant.

In this hands-on demo, you'll configure a device running Hecate and use it to passively sniff serial communications between two systems. Then, you can extend your device using Hecate, first into a datalogger to capture UART traffic, and then into a payload injector to spoof communications. Finally, you'll see how to implement a full implant-in-the-middle capable of modifying data in transit.

Hecate lowers the barrier to entry for developing embedded implants while remaining flexible enough for advanced research and rapid prototyping. Attendees will leave with a working understanding of UART interception, manipulation, and exploitation, and a framework they can use in their own work.

tool_name: INFLEX: Cross-Format Malware Analysis and Correlation Framework
description:
INFLEX is a heterogeneous malware analysis framework designed to analyze, enrich, and correlate malicious artifacts across multiple file formats. The system supports PE, ELF, shellcode, and malicious document analysis while combining static analysis, emulation, optional dynamic sandboxing, and threat intelligence enrichment into a single unified workflow.

Many existing malware analysis tools focus on a single artifact type or rely primarily on one analysis technique such as sandbox execution or static disassembly. INFLEX was designed to bridge this gap by normalizing analysis outputs across artifact types and enabling analysts to correlate relationships between samples that would otherwise remain disconnected.

The framework performs deep feature extraction including structural metadata, disassembly analysis, behavioral extraction through emulation, and function-level hashing to identify shared code structures across malware variants. Analysis results are enriched with external threat intelligence and stored in a scalable database that enables automated and analyst correlation across large malware collections.

By combining heterogeneous artifact support, multi-modal analysis, and large-scale correlation capabilities, INFLEX provides analysts with a powerful platform for identifying malware relationships, uncovering shared infrastructure, and accelerating malware triage and investigation workflows at scale.

tool_name: LoRaCraft – Crafting Attacks for LoRaWAN Networks
description:
LoRaWAN is deployed in billions of IoT devices; smart meters, agricultural sensors, industrial automation, medical telemetry. It's also consistently misconfigured, poorly understood by the teams that run it, and almost entirely absent from the standard pen tester's toolkit.

LoraCraft is a LoRaWAN security assessment framework built for practical use in real audits. It covers the full protocol stack: join request replay against LoRaWAN 1.0.x DevNonce weaknesses, AES-CTR bit-flipping, authenticated packet injection with known session keys, energy depletion via confirmed uplink flooding and MAC command abuse, and rogue gateway operation over the Semtech UDP packet forwarder protocol.

The tool consumes traffic three ways: PCAP captures of UDP port 1700 gateway traffic, MQTT subscriptions to ChirpStack or TTN, or live capture through its own built-in fake gateway. Everything is stored per-session, and a web UI outputs findings with traffic visualizations and HTML/JSON/PDF reports.

SDR-based physical layer attacks ;continuous, reactive, and selective jamming; PHY sniffing via gr-lora are integrated and operational with GNU Radio and appropriate hardware, but the network level attack surface is fully accessible without any of it.

Most LoRaWAN deployments in the field are still running 1.0.x, using ABP with static keys hardcoded in firmware, disabled frame counter checks for "convenience," and vendor default AppKeys that have never been rotated. LoraCraft finds all of this in a workflow that fits alongside the tools you already use.

tool_name: Precogly: Open Source Threat Modeling for AI-Assisted Security
description:
Precogly is the open-source alternative to commercial, enterprise-scale threat modeling tools.
It includes:
- community-driven threat libraries
- a full DFD editor with reusable templates
- a unified threat analysis workspace
- integrations with taxonomies like LINDDUN, CAPEC and ATT&CK as well as compliance standards like PCI-DSS, NIST etc.
- Hooks to allow AI-Assisted threat modeling to happen at an enterprise scale
- Reporting views catering to security teams, risk managers and compliance managers

This demo walks attendees through several capabilities that don't exist in open-source alternatives today, and shows how Precogly removes the three biggest barriers to threat modeling adoption: cost, expertise and AI-agent compatibility.

tool_name: ThreatXtension: AI-Powered Browser Extension Security Analysis Framework
description:
ThreatXtension is a novel automated framework for Chrome extension security analysis that combines static application security testing (SAST) with
large language model (LLM) powered threat intelligence. Unlike traditional static analyzers that produce rule-based alerts, ThreatXtension employs a
context-aware AI architecture to assess permission risk, detect obfuscated malicious patterns, and generate natural language threat summaries.

The tool introduces a LangGraph workflow pipeline that orchestrates extension acquisition from Chrome Web Store, manifest parsing (V2/V3),
parallel multi-analyzer execution, and LLM-powered result synthesis. Our research contribution includes: (1) custom Semgrep rulesets targeting
browser extension-specific attack vectors with MITRE ATT&CK mappings, (2) a hybrid rule-based + LLM architecture for context-aware permissions
analysis against sensitive domain watchlists, and (3) automated executive summary generation that bridges technical findings with strategic risk
assessment.

ThreatXtension supports multiple LLM backends (IBM WatsonX, OpenAI, local Ollama) and provides three interfaces: CLI for automation, web UI for
interactive analysis, and FastMCP integration for conversational security research. The tool addresses the growing threat landscape of malicious
browser extensions, particularly targeting banking fraud and credential theft patterns.

tool_name: BadZure: Building Cloud Attack Labs with AI
description:
BadZure is an open source tool that uses AI to build misconfigured cloud lab environments with realistic, traversable attack paths. Security practitioners describe their desired scenario in natural language and BadZure translates the prompt into a fully provisioned Entra ID and Azure environment complete with identities, groups, applications, cloud resources, permission assignments, and intentional misconfigurations that produce exploitable privilege escalation chains.

The generated environments mirror organic enterprise tenants: identities accumulate roles and permissions, groups inherit access across resources, and managed identities bridge cloud infrastructure to the identity layer. On top of this realistic baseline, BadZure layers attack paths that chain compromised identities to high privilege targets through service principal abuse, credential theft from Key Vaults and Storage Accounts, managed identity token theft, and more.

BadZure deploys everything through Terraform, making environments fully repeatable and disposable. Security teams can spin up a lab, traverse the attack paths, observe the telemetry, and tear it all down, then prompt a different scenario and start again. This makes it a practical platform for purple team exercises, detection engineering, hands on cloud security training, and CTF events.

tool_name: Brutus: Modern Multi-Protocol Credential Testing in Go
description:
Network credential testing remains a critical capability for penetration testers and red team operators, yet existing tools like THC Hydra suffer from decades of technical debt: complex dependency chains requiring libssh-dev, libmysqlclient-dev, and platform-specific compilation issues that break regularly. These legacy tools offer no native integration with modern reconnaissance workflows, forcing operators to write brittle shell scripts for format conversion between discovery and credential testing phases.

Brutus addresses these pain points with a purpose-built Go implementation delivered as a single binary with zero external dependencies. The tool supports 20+ protocols (SSH, MySQL, PostgreSQL, MSSQL, Redis, SMB, RDP, MongoDB, and more) with native JSON streaming for seamless integration with fingerprintx and naabu pipelines—enabling complete network credential audits via simple pipe operations. Unique features include embedded SSH badkeys (Vagrant, F5 BIG-IP CVE-2012-1493, ExaGrid CVE-2016-1561) compiled directly into the binary, RDP credential testing with automatic sticky keys backdoor detection via a Rust-to-WASM-to-wazero architecture that preserves the zero-CGO single-binary design, and optional LLM-powered credential suggestions that analyze HTTP responses to recommend vendor-specific default passwords for discovered admin panels. Brutus runs identically on Linux, macOS, and Windows, and can be imported as a Go library for custom security automation without subprocess execution overhead.

Attendees will experience live credential testing across a simulated corporate network, from port discovery with naabu to service identification with fingerprintx to multi-protocol credential validation with Brutus, all demonstrated in a single pipeline. The demo will walk through the LLM-controlled browser identifying and authenticating against unknown admin panels in real time, SSH badkey spraying across infrastructure, sticky keys backdoor detection on compromised RDP hosts, and side-by-side comparison with Hydra highlighting the dependency and integration pain points Brutus eliminates. Visitors will leave with practical knowledge of pipeline-native reconnaissance and sample configurations for integrating Brutus into their security testing workflows.

tool_name: FAInd my XPC: Automated Discovery of Privilege Escalation via macOS XPC Trust Boundaries - powered by LLM
description: XPC Hunter is an automated macOS XPC attack surface discovery and privilege escalation validation framework. It identifies exploitable privileged XPC interfaces across all installed macOS applications by combining static binary analysis (otool protocol extraction, strings-based service name discovery), dynamic runtime enumeration via CDHash cache exploitation with NIB-injected JXA payloads, and AI-powered semantic scoring using Claude. The tool exploits a systemic vulnerability class: macOS applications that expose root-level XPC services protected only by CDHash-based trust, which can be bypassed entirely from userland without modifying any signed binary. XPC Hunter automates the full pipeline — from app discovery through NIB injection type classification, runtime service validation, method signature extraction, and AI-ranked attack surface reporting — reducing what previously required hours of manual reverse engineering per target to minutes across an entire macOS installation. Using the same underlying technique, we achieved local privilege escalation against Kandji MDM (permanent agent deactivation) and the market-leading EDR products.

tool_name: MSSQLHound - Identify, Visualize, and Navigate MSSQL Attack Paths in BloodHound
description: MSSQLHound enumerates Microsoft SQL Server principals and permissions at the domain, server, and database levels, processes the relationships between them, identifies abusable attack paths, and maps and connects them to the BloodHound graph for interactive exploration and querying.

tool_name: PwnSat 2.0: The Vulnerable Satellite Hacking Platform for Learning Through Research
description:
The aerospace industry is rapidly shifting toward software-defined satellites, yet the "security by obscurity" myth persists. PwnSat 2.0 is the major evolution of the first open-source, vulnerable-by-design aerospace cybersecurity platform. While version 1.0 focused on RF communication attacks, this new release for Black Hat USA introduces **Enterprise-Grade Mission Control** integration and **Full-Chain Mission Compromise** scenarios.

PwnSat 2.0 bridges the gap between hardware hacking and complex space operations. It features a physical 1U CubeSat, a LoRa/FSK Ground Station, and now, native support for Aerospace's enterprise Ground Station, the industry standard for Command, Control, and Communications (C3).

We will demonstrate how an attacker can move laterally from a compromised Ground Station backend to gain unauthorized satellite control. Attendees will witness live exploitations of CCSDS and AX.25 protocols, firmware memory corruption on the flight computer, and the hijacking of real-time telemetry streams within a professional C3 environment. PwnSat 2.0 provides the community with a high-fidelity sandbox to practice offensive and defensive tactics under the SPARTA (Space Attack Research & Tactics Analysis) framework, now scaled for hardware-level research.

tool_name: pymsi - Interactive MSI Installer Analysis in Python and the Browser
description:
pymsi is a pure Python library for parsing, analyzing, and extracting files from Windows Installer (MSI) packages. It provides direct access to MSI database tables, embedded streams, and installer metadata, enabling security researchers to inspect installer behavior. A fully client-side web-based version wraps the pymsi library in a familiar lessmsi-style UI, providing a convenient tool that can be used from any operating system to inspect and extract files from MSI installers.

Unlike other tools that are either Windows-only (lessmsi, orca) or primarily for Linux/macOS (msitools), pymsi works on any system with a suitable Python interpreter, making it a flexible foundation for integration with automated installer inspection workflows that work on any operating system, and making it easy to inspect potentially malicious MSI installers in a sandboxed environment.

tool_name: StegoScan
description:
Bad actors have long used hidden information in many forms, for malicious purposes, continuously evolving their methods over time. To counter these threats, our detection software must also evolve, ensuring effective identification and mitigation. Heading these threats is stenography, the practice of concealing messages or content within other non-suspicious data. Previously steganography detection tools have focused on limited sets of file types at a surface level and require manual processing leading to unknown extents of undetected illicit content, and potentially wasteful labor. Which is why a better solution had to be developed: StegoScan.py is a powerful, next-generation tool that automates steganography detection in websites, web servers, and local directories, by integrating AI-driven object and deep file text recognition analysis. StegoScan.py is a comprehensive tool that is capable of scanning and scraping websites across a broad range of formats simultaneously with deep file extraction.

The tool boasts website and web server scanning capabilities, making it invaluable for security researchers monitoring illicit data exchanges or law enforcement tracking cybercriminals. A single command can analyze entire domains or IP ranges, retrieving and inspecting suspicious media and documents for hidden communications. Whether it's detecting covert exchanges in dark web marketplaces, identifying embedded propaganda in misinformation campaigns, or revealing concealed instructions within terrorist networks, StegoScan.py offers visibility into steganographic threats. Stegoscan.py integrates numerous AI models that enhance text detection by overcoming the former challenges of noise, distortions, and unconventional fonts, allowing forensic analysts, cybersecurity professionals, and law enforcement agencies to extract text from compromised media with increased confidence.

By combining multiple steganalysis techniques into a toolkit, StegoScan.py provides a detailed and multi-layered analysis of files, offering security teams, digital forensics experts, and cybersecurity researchers a cutting-edge solution to an evolving digital threat. As steganography techniques become more sophisticated, traditional tools fall short—StegoScan.py ensures organizations stay ahead of bad actors by detecting what others miss. This is accomplished by automatically scanning websites, organizing tests, utilizing AI to remove the need for manual inspection, and combining many mainstream tools and tests to ensure detection across a wide range of files and steganography techniques. In testing, StegoScan was able to scan a website and find hidden messages embedded in an image that was embedded in a pdf linked to the original webpage. This shows the depth and abilities that this tool offers, whereas operating with a previously developed workflow the user would have had to download the PDF manually, extract the suspected images and then run individual tests to uncover the stenography.

tool_name: Suzaku by Yamato Security
description: Suzaku (朱雀) is an open-source, Sigma-based threat hunting and DFIR timeline generator for cloud logs, developed by Yamato Security — the same team behind the widely adopted Windows event log analysis tool Hayabusa. Written in Rust for memory safety and high performance, Suzaku scans JSON and compressed JSON.gz cloud log files using multithreading to rapidly surface attacker activity across massive datasets. This major release marks a significant expansion of Suzaku's cloud coverage: AWS CloudTrail analysis has been substantially enhanced with deeper support for new API categories, improved GeoIP enrichment, and expanded Sigma correlation rule coverage, while Azure log support has been introduced for the first time, bringing the same fast-forensics timeline and signature-based detection capabilities to Microsoft cloud environments. Suzaku is cross-platform, running on Windows, Linux, and macOS, and outputs results in CSV, JSON, and JSONL formats for easy integration with existing DFIR workflows.

tool_name: Vulnhalla 2.0: LLM-Guided Triage of CodeQL Findings
description:
Vulnhalla is an open-source pipeline that runs CodeQL at scale and uses an LLM agent to automatically triage findings as true positive or false positive. It reduces the static analysis haystack using two novel methods: (1) extracting the exact context the LLM needs from the CodeQL database using structured CSV artifacts for very fast retrieval, and (2) a reasoning engine that drives the model through reviewer-style, high-level checks (reachability, controllability, sanitization, boundary conditions, etc.) instead of brittle one-shot prompts using a guided-question technique.

Vulnhalla 1.0 supported C/C++ and was a huge success in practice, helping identify real-world vulnerabilities in large projects such as the Linux kernel, FFmpeg, and Redis, and it was also used in the discovery of CVE-2025-60021 (CVSS 9.8), a critical remote command injection in Apache bRPC heap profiler endpoint.

Vulnhalla 2.0 expands beyond C/C++ with first-class support for Python and JavaScript, broadening coverage to major web-development ecosystems, and it supports local and closed-source analysis (build the CodeQL database locally and run the full pipeline without relying on GitHub-hosted projects).

tool_name: CyberArkHound
description: CyberArkHound is an open-source security assessment tool written in Go that exports CyberArk PVWA data — users, groups, safes, accounts, platforms, and permissions — into a BloodHound-compatible OpenGraph JSON file. By bridging CyberArk's Privileged Access Management (PAM) data with BloodHound's attack path analysis engine, it enables security teams to visualize and query PAM privilege relationships alongside traditional Active Directory attack paths. This makes previously opaque CyberArk permission structures queryable with Cypher and visible as attack graphs, exposing direct credential access, privilege escalation paths, dual control weaknesses, and credential chain dependencies that are otherwise invisible in standard PAM auditing workflows.

tool_name: Dradis Framework: Intelligent Automation for collaboration and reporting
description:
Dradis centralises findings, evidence, and attack narratives in a single portal combining output from Nessus, Burp Suite, Nikto, and 47+ other scanners with manual research to simplify collaboration and reporting across the whole team.

Recent updates include context-aware LLM assistance with Bring Your Own LLM (Dradis Echo) so everything stays on your infrastructure, agents, a prompt library for repeatable AI workflows, dark mode, REST API-based scanner uploads, in-app QA workflows with new inline commenting, and a MITRE ATT&CK coverage calculator. Easier to deploy than ever through Docker, and more capable once you're in.

Free + Open Source (GPLv2). Self-hosted. No data leaves your environment.

tool_name: From Breakthrough to Completeness: arkdecompiler - The Decompiler for HarmonyOS NEXT
description:
Following its official release, Huawei's HarmonyOS NEXT has undergone explosive growth, with its user base rapidly approaching 50 million and projected to exceed 100 million by the end of 2026. Operating independently of the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), its unique native stack—from the Harmony kernel to the Ark-Bytecode execution environment—presents a persistent and expanding challenge for the global security community. To address the critical need for security auditing in this surging ecosystem, we previously introduced arkdecompiler, a specialized engine for reconstructing ArkTS source code from Panda Bytecode. After establishing the core framework at Black Hat USA 2025 and demonstrating initial support for fundamental constructs (such as loops, classes, etc.) at Black Hat Asia 2026, we now present a major evolution of the framework: the transition from a structural PoC to production-grade semantic completeness.

While our previous work laid the foundational architecture, real-world HarmonyOS applications rely on a vast array of specialized instructions and complex, modern language features that were not yet fully addressed. This session introduces a significant leap in arkdecompiler's capabilities, focusing on exhaustive instruction set support, sophisticated semantic reconstruction, and industrial-scale automated validation.

Key Technical Advancements in This Update:

A) Full-Spectrum Syntax & Instruction Mapping
- Contextual Property Access: Support for loading and storing properties via this and super contexts, including Private Class Fields and __proto__ attribute settings.
- Interpreter-Level Semantic Equivalents: Providing equivalent functional sequences for complex Asynchronous operations and Arrow Functions that mirror the interpreter's internal execution logic.
- Generator State-Machine Deconstruction: Resolving the suspend/resume logic triggered by the yield keyword into equivalent high-level generator semantics.
- Advanced Object & Array Semantics: Recovery of Spread-based object creation, Destructuring assignments with rest properties, and dynamic Key-to-Property mapping.
- Enhanced Function & Module Logic: Support for Static/Dynamic Imports, Rest Parameter copying, and accessing the arguments keyword in underlying frames.
- Super-Call Complexity: Accurate mapping of Spread-based super() calls and constructor invocations to ensure correct variadic argument handling.
- Specialized Literal & Metadata Support: Resolution of GetTemplateObject instructions, digitized RegExp flags, and Getter/Setter accessor functions
- Iterator: Handling for-in/for-of iterators instructions for precise try-catch-finally reconstruction.

B) High-Fidelity Semantic Analysis & Logical Optimization
- Path-Sensitive Deconvolution: A new analysis engine to handle variations in lexical environments across disparate execution paths, ensuring analysis integrity in non-linear logic.
- SSA-to-Source Transformation: Robust Phi-instruction elimination to resolve variable versioning and reconstruct clean high-level source code.
- Internal Argument Pruning: Identification and removal of interpreter-injected parameters, restoring clean and original function signatures.
- Branch Logic Simplification: Applying condition inversion and boolean logic optimization to transform convoluted conditional branches into structured code.
- Cross-Unit Isolation: Treating classes as independent analysis units to ensure accurate member function and property reconstruction.

C) HarmonyOS-Native Primitives & System-Level Adaptation
- Advanced Concurrency via Sendable Objects: To overcome the heavy overhead of cross-thread communication in traditional JS engines—which typically requires moving logic to the Native layer via transferable objects—HarmonyOS NEXT introduces Sendable objects and shared lexical environments. Our decompiler implements specialized support for these primitives, accurately supporting the pass-by-reference logic and concurrent communication patterns unique to this ecosystem.

- Interpreter-Aligned Semantic Mapping: We implement robust support for specialized bytecode categories, including CallRuntime and Throw-class instructions. By aligning with the interpreter's internal execution patterns, our engine provides equivalent functional representations for these operations, ensuring that system-level service calls and exception control flows are accurately represented in the decompiled output.

- Symbolic Hierarchy Decoding: Specialized logic for decoding HarmonyOS-specific naming prefixes within the internal instruction stream. This enables the precise restoration of class affiliations, function nesting relationships, and complex scope hierarchies that define the application's structural architecture.

- Internal Argument Pruning: Identification and selective removal of interpreter-injected parameters (such as internal pointers for context or closures) that are essential for execution but redundant for source-level readability. This process is vital for restoring clean and original function signatures that reflect the developer's intent.

D) Industrial-Scale Validation & Automated Pipeline
- Automated Batch Testing Pipeline: We have developed a custom automated framework tailored for the HarmonyOS ecosystem. This pipeline automatically identifies TypeScript and JavaScript files within expansive datasets and ensures successful compilation into Panda bytecode before invoking the decompiler. By monitoring the AST construction process and capturing any parsing failures, the pipeline effectively serves as a structural robustness validator.

- Result Classification & Analysis: To handle the immense volume of data, the pipeline implements a systematic classification of compilation and decompilation results. By categorizing successful parses and specific failure modes, we can efficiently perform targeted analysis and prioritize the resolution of the most critical structural issues.

- Massive Dataset Assembly: Leveraging this automated pipeline, we have processed an extensive validation suite of 86,150 samples, categorized into two primary pillars:
- Customized ArkTS Repository (third_party_typescript): A collection of 19,136 TypeScript and 13,756 JavaScript samples derived from official TypeScript sources and optimized by Huawei for the native ArkTS environment.
- Standardized JS Suite (test262): 53,258 JavaScript test cases from the industry-standard ECMAScript compliance suite.

- Active Edge-Case Resolution Phase: We are currently in an active phase of identifying and resolving thousands of corner cases revealed by this massive-scale testing. By ensuring the decompiler can successfully reconstruct complex, real-world code structures without internal parsing errors, we are pushing the tool toward production-grade reliability and robust performance against the rapidly evolving HarmonyOS application landscape.

tool_name: LogonTracer v2: Faster Malicious Windows Logon Investigations with AI Agent
description:
LogonTracer v2 is an open-source tool that helps defenders quickly detect, understand, and operationalize suspicious Windows logons in large enterprise environments.

For analysts, one of the biggest challenges in Windows investigations is that malicious logons are often buried in massive volumes of noisy event data. LogonTracer v2 helps solve this by organizing authentication activity into an intuitive graph of users and hosts, highlighting suspicious behavior, and reducing large event sets into a much smaller number of high-value leads. Instead of spending hours manually reviewing raw logs, defenders can quickly identify where to look first, what happened, and how suspicious activity is connected across accounts and systems.

LogonTracer v2 adds practical AI-assisted workflows for real-world operations. Its AI agent can automatically investigate Windows Event Logs to detect malicious logon patterns, its LLM-based summarization can turn complex log activity into understandable investigation summaries, and its Sigma rule generation capability helps defenders turn discovered behaviors into reusable detections for future monitoring. Together, these capabilities make the tool useful not only for finding suspicious logons, but also for helping teams understand incidents faster and improve their detection coverage over time.

In this session, we will demonstrate how LogonTracer v2 can be used to ingest Windows Event Logs, detect suspicious logons with AI assistance, summarize investigation results, and generate Sigma rules that defenders can bring back into their operational environment. The session will focus on practical analyst benefits, incident response workflow, and how the tool reduces time-to-understanding during Windows investigations.

tool_name: Nemesis 2.2
description: Nemesis is an open-source, centralized data processing platform that ingests, enriches, and allows collaborative analysis (with humans and AI) of files collected during offensive security assessments. Nemesis 2.2 builds on last year's ground-up rewrite with major new capabilities for processing data at scale. Nemesis can now ingest full disk images and large forensic containers, automatically carving and enriching extracted files. A complete DPAPI auto-decryption pipeline handles everything from classic DPAPI through Chromium's latest v3 app-bound encryption, automatically linking the necessary files to decrypt browser cookies and saved logins. Optional LLM agents address the false positive problem at scale through automated finding triage, credential extraction, document summarization, and a natural language chatbot for querying the Nemesis datastore. New file linking, per-host reporting, and significant performance optimizations round out the release.

tool_name: notyet: Automated IAM Persistence Analysis Through AWS Eventual Consistency Abuse
description: When incident responders revoke compromised AWS credentials, they believe the threat has been neutralized. However, AWS IAM operates as an eventually consistent system where changes such as key deletion, policy detachment, or role removal require seconds to propagate until the AWS authorization system picks up the changes. notyet takes advantage of this window to maintain access indefinitely, automatically rotating credentials and restoring permissions faster than defenders apply revocation. The tool is integrated in a web interface that helps defenders and researchers test and validate their containment techniques against the persistence techniques.

tool_name: ShellWasp: Creating Shellcode with Windows Syscalls
description:
Direct Windows syscalls have become extremely popular in offensive security, but unfortunately almost all of that work has been aimed at higher-level implants rather than shellcode. In shellcode, the problem is (a lot) harder: system service numbers (SSNs) change across the countless OS builds. There are a lot of other issues too - Wow64 mechancis can differ a lot from Windows 7 versus modern Windows 10/11, and building the required structures in position-independent assembly is significantly more painful than doing the same thing in C or C++. ShellWasp is built as a dedicated tool for generating Windows syscall shellcode in 32-bit WoW64, rather than yet another syscall helper for higher-level projects. It won't do all the work for you - but it will help you overcome a lot of the hurdles.

ShellWasp automates the creation of compact syscall shellcode templates and removes some of the painful low-level setup that would make pure syscall shellcode impractical. ShellWasp identifies the target OS build at runtime, generates a syscall array so the correct SSNs and manages reuse of syscalls within that array. This allows the user to focus on building the syscall shellcode, obtaining much greater stealth, rather than trying to focus on booking mechanics that could cause it to fail.

ShellWasp has introduced some powerful capabilities to help with stealth. In addition to classic PEB-based discovery of OSBuild, ShellWasp adds alternative methods such as User_Shared_Data and the PEB-via-r12 approach. It also includes some totally novel ways to invoke WoW64 syscalls beyond the standard fs:[0xc0] path, with one method for Windows 7 and two for Windows 10/11. These give users greater flexibility in how syscall shellcode is built, providing stealthier ways of executing syscalls in a shellcode context.

In 2026, the tool has been updated to produce illustrative, sample values - both from an offline mode and generated on-the-fly with optional AI. That can help people immensely who are starting out and need help. There will be others special new surprises to debut at Arsenal USA 2026!

Arsenal 2026 will provide a rare opportunity to see and talk about ShellWasp and gain insight on using Windows syscalls in shellcode. For exploit developers and red teamers, ShellWasp opens a path that has historically been too difficult and too labor-intensive to use in practice. For those who have mastered writing shellcode, ShellWasp is a must.

tool_name: VulnZoo: A Complete Vulnerable IoT Ecosystem for Security Research and Training
description: VulnZoo is an open-source ecosystem of vulnerable devices designed to fill the gap in practical cybersecurity training in embedded, medical, industrial and automotive environments. Unlike current platforms that focus on isolated components, VulnZoo models a complete IoT product from device firmware to mobile applications and cloud services allowing the study of realistic attack chains between multiple components.

tool_name: Bastet: An Infrastructure for Benchmarking LLM Smart Contract Auditing
description:
Bastet is a security infrastructure that integrates a comprehensive dataset of common smart contract vulnerabilities in DeFi with an AI-driven automated detection process.
It focuses on vulnerabilities that are common yet difficult to detect using static analysis tools, issues that are frequently classified as medium to high risk in audit competitions and often causing financial losses.

The Bastet dataset encompasses real-world vulnerabilities observed both on-chain and in audit competitions, providing a foundation for developing and evaluating automated detection techniques.
Through tailored detection workflows, Bastet enhances AI's accuracy in identifying these complex vulnerabilities, aiming to optimize security lifecycle management, from development and auditing to ongoing monitoring.

tool_name: Emulate cloud-native attacks with Stratus Red Team
description:
What attacks are used by threat actors in cloud environments? How to reproduce them easily to ensure that our threat detection mechanisms are working as expected?

Stratus Red Team provides a solution to these two questions. With support for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Entra ID Kubernetes, it allows threat detection and cloud security engineering team to reproduce common cloud attacks in a self-contained manner, along with actionable detection insights.

tool_name: MLOKit: MLOps Attack Toolkit
description:
MLOKit is an open-source C# toolkit that can be used to attack MLOps platforms by taking advantage of available REST APIs. The tool allows a user to specify an attack module along with valid credentials for a target MLOps platform. MLOKit currently supports Azure ML, Amazon SageMaker, Google Cloud Vertex AI, MLFlow, BigML, and Palantir AIP. Attack modules include reconnaissance, training data theft, model theft, model poisoning, and notebook attacks.

This release introduces 9 new modules that significantly expand MLOKit's attack surface coverage. New capabilities include enumerating ML compute instances and their SSH configurations, adding attacker SSH keys to compute instances for persistent access, creating malicious training jobs for arbitrary code execution, harvesting credentials from training job variables and log files, downloading Docker build files from ML environments that may contain embedded secrets, and executing code directly within JupyterLab notebook instances via WebSocket connections. These new modules target Azure ML and Amazon SageMaker, extending MLOKit's capabilities from data and model theft into compute access, credential harvesting, and code execution within ML training infrastructure.

tool_name: MSCodePhish - Dynamic Device Code Phishing Framework
description:
MSCodePhish is a red‑team toolkit that turns Microsoft's Device Code OAuth flow into an embeddable phishing primitive that works inside any lure (e.g., "grab your coupon," "unlock access," etc.). Instead of pre‑generating device codes and racing against the usual 15‑minute timeout, MSCodePhish exposes a simple API endpoint that phishing pages can call via JavaScript (XHR/fetch) at the exact moment a victim opens the page. The tool then generates a fresh device code on demand, returns it to the phishing page (e.g., rendered as a "coupon code"), and instructs the user to complete the login on the legitimate Microsoft device login portal using that code.
Behind the scenes, MSCodePhish continuously polls Microsoft's token endpoint for that device code and, once the victim finishes authentication, captures the resulting refresh token and related claims (tenant, user, etc.). From its web UI, operators can track active campaigns, monitor which lures are converting, and use captured refresh tokens to request new access tokens for different resources (ARM, Key Vault, Graph, Storage, or custom scopes) in real time. Because the code is generated only when the phishing HTML is actually loaded, MSCodePhish effectively sidesteps device‑code expiration issues and enables more realistic, flexible phishing flows that closely mimic benign "promo code" or "access code" UX patterns.
The framework is aimed at offensive security teams and researchers who want to test how easily users can be manipulated into completing the device code flow on a legitimate Microsoft page, and to demonstrate the downstream impact of a single successful device‑code phish in modern Azure/M365 environments.

https://github.com/TROUBLE-1/MSCodePhish

tool_name: Nogitsune: eBPF-Based Anti-VM Detection for Linux Malware Analysis
description:
Nogitsune is the first eBPF-based anti-VM detection toolkit for Linux. For nine years, Windows analysts had runtime tools like VBoxCloak while Linux analysts were stuck recompiling hypervisors. Malware like Amnesia detects VMs and executes rm -rf / to destroy analysis environments. Traditional Linux solutions require patching QEMU source, rebuilding SeaBIOS, and hypervisor access most analysts don't have.
Nogitsune uses eBPF to intercept file reads and syscalls at the kernel level, rewriting hardware identifiers before malware receives them. One command transforms an exposed VirtualBox VM into a spoofed "Dell OptiPlex" that defeats file-based detection used by Amnesia, XorDDoS, cryptominers, and IoT botnets. The toolkit intercepts 10 DMI file paths, spoofs MAC addresses across three query methods (file read, ioctl, netlink), hides processes including itself, and modifies disk, CPU, and memory attributes.
The demo shows live malware detonation. Amnesia executes safely after reading spoofed Dell DMI values instead of VirtualBox identifiers. Attendees test their own samples with strace showing intercepted syscalls. Hardware instruction detection (CPUID, RDTSC) cannot be intercepted by eBPF but is rarely used by real Linux malware.
Runtime deployment on stock kernels. No hypervisor access. No VM restart.

tool_name: Practical Ransomware Detection on macOS (via Math, not AI)
description:
Ransomware remains a serious threat to macOS users, especially as Apple devices continue to gain traction in the enterprise. Despite its many variants, most ransomware shares a fundamental behavior: rapidly transforming user files into encrypted data.

This talk presents a practical, math-driven approach to generically detecting and stopping ransomware on macOS. While this approach builds on established ideas, it is now far more practical with Apple's Endpoint Security framework. By leveraging Endpoint Security and entropy-based analysis, we can distinguish benign file activity from encryption, and further differentiate encrypted data from compressed data using simple mathematical heuristics. This approach avoids signatures and machine learning, instead relying on observable behavior and measurable properties of data.

Our approach is then implemented in a free, open-source tool, dubbed "RansomWhere?" which has been tested against macOS ransomware samples!

tool_name: pymsi - Interactive MSI Installer Analysis in Python and the Browser
description:
pymsi is a pure Python library for parsing, analyzing, and extracting files from Windows Installer (MSI) packages. It provides direct access to MSI database tables, embedded streams, and installer metadata, enabling security researchers to inspect installer behavior. A fully client-side web-based version wraps the pymsi library in a familiar lessmsi-style UI, providing a convenient tool that can be used from any operating system to inspect and extract files from MSI installers.

Unlike other tools that are either Windows-only (lessmsi, orca) or primarily for Linux/macOS (msitools), pymsi works on any system with a suitable Python interpreter, making it a flexible foundation for integration with automated installer inspection workflows that work on any operating system, and making it easy to inspect potentially malicious MSI installers in a sandboxed environment.

tool_name: Suricata 8: Discover the Difference in Network Detection
description:
Suricata is a high-performance, open source network analysis and threat detection software widely used by most private and public organizations, and embedded by major vendors to protect their assets. Suricata has been an example of innovation, constant improvements, community collaboration, and has been at the forefront of network detection evolution for the past 16 years.

As part of that journey, it has advanced to different modes of operation – Intrusion Detection / Intrusion Prevention / Firewall / Network Security Monitoring / PCAP logging with industry-leading performance. Suricata provides network protocol, flow, alert, anomaly logs, file extraction, and PCAP capture at very high speeds.

After 2 years of community and consortium development, Suricata 8 brings many advanced features and possibilities to the Blue Teams and network defenders. To name a few: new mode of operation (Firewall), logging improvements, complete Lua overhaul, 8 new protocols - mDNS, LDAP, DoH (DNS-over-HTTPS), WebSocket, and others, plus 100+ new detection fields/keywords, hundreds of new logging fields, bidirectional rules, CPU affinity, performance, and more.

tool_name: Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills
description:
AI coding agents from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft support the agentskills.io open standard but ship with zero cybersecurity domain knowledge. This project fills that gap: 734 open-source skills across 37 security subdomains, mapping 127+ MITRE ATT&CK techniques, with tool-specific commands, NIST CSF alignment, and step-by-step procedural workflows backed by 1,000+ runnable Python scripts.

Live demonstration covers four scenarios. First, loading skills into Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Codex CLI and watching each agent perform memory forensics with Volatility3. Second, a side-by-side comparison where the same agent attempts malware triage, threat hunting, and incident response with and without skills. Third, walking the ATT&CK Navigator heatmap showing technique coverage -- strongest in Credential Access (~85%) and Lateral Movement (~80%), with honest gaps in Impact (~40%). Fourth, attendees pick any skill, load it into their preferred agent, and test it live.

Every skill follows agentskills.io progressive disclosure: YAML frontmatter for discovery, structured workflows, and supporting scripts. Apache-2.0 licensed and installable via a single npx command.

Attendees leave with cybersecurity skills loaded into their own AI agent, ready for real security work.

tool_name: APTL: Advanced Purple Team Labs
description: APTL is an OSS, Docker-based purple team lab with an OSS SOC stack, MCPs, and scenario system that allows users to pit agents against each other, research red and blue team agent behaviour, and test their enhancement strategies. The lab runs on commodity hardware with consumer-grade AI services and captures all telemetry to support research and review. MIT licensed.

tool_name: EMBA – The product security analysis framework
description:
IoT (Internet of Things), ICS (Industrial Control Systems) and OT (Operational Technology) are the buzzwords for networked devices which our modern society is based on. In this area, the operating systems that are in place are summarized with the term firmware. The devices themselves, also called embedded systems, are essential in the private and industrial environments as well as in the so-called critical infrastructure.
Security testing of these systems is quite complex as the tester must deal with different architectures, optimized operating systems and special protocols. EMBA is an open-source firmware security analyzer with the goal of simplifying and optimizing the complex task of firmware security analysis. EMBA supports the tester with the automated detection of known vulnerabilities on binary level. This goes far beyond the plain CVE detection: With EMBA you always know which public exploits are available for the target firmware. Besides the detection of already known vulnerabilities, EMBA also supports the tester on the next unknown (0-day) vulnerability. There are many other features built into EMBA, such as fully automated firmware extraction, identification of vulnerabilities in scripting languages or hard-coded credentials. To go the extra mile EMBA also has AI integration that supports the tester with the identification of more complex vulnerabilities and better understanding of the discovered vulnerabilities.
EMBA is the open-source firmware scanner, built to make IoT more secure.

tool_name: Tengu Marauder Vanguard Version 2.0
description:
The Tengu Marauder Vanguard 2.0 is an open-source robotic cybersecurity platform designed for physical red team operations and assessing vulnerabilities in wireless networks. The platform utilizes the Raspberry Pi 5, enabling an operator to deploy and manage units throughout a designated environment from a single interface. This interface, developed on Flask, features a tailored framework. It offers real-time visualization of targets, integrated network scanning, and cohesive management of units.

Version 2.0 introduces significantly more features compared to the original Tengu Marauder. Protocol coverage encompasses Bluetooth scanning and SDR-based RF tools. The integration of an ESP32-C5 module introduces dual-band 2.4/5 GHz WiFi testing, enabling you to evaluate contemporary wireless environments that were once inaccessible. The Hailo AI HAT 2 and Fusion HAT+ work together to bring AI inference directly to the robot, allowing it to analyze targets and make decisions on its own without needing the cloud.

A Banana Pi BPI-R4 operating on OpenWrt manages network coordination among various units. It serves as the primary network controller for the platform, offering access point functionality, traffic routing, and reliable connectivity for all deployed units.

Tengu Marauder Vanguard 2.0 is designed for cyber operators with authorization, wireless security researchers, and individuals who assess physical and RF attack surfaces in corporate and IoT environments.

tool_name: ARAY: Benign Binary Synthesis for Signature Validation Without the Malware
description:
Aray generates non-malicious executable files that match YARA rules, no malware samples required. Given a .yar file, it produces a benign Linux ELF, Windows PE, or generic binary artifact that triggers the rule, enabling security teams to validate detection logic safely and at scale.

Under the hood, Aray runs a nine-node LangGraph pipeline backed by an LLM (GPT-4.1 by default, or a local SLM such as phi4:14b via Ollama).
The pipeline normalizes the rule into a form amenable to extraction, then extracts string patterns and integer constants, and finally synthesizes a binary that satisfies every structural constraint — byte-offset placement, section alignment, uint16/uint32 constant encoding, wide-string (UTF-16LE) embedding, and Windows PE header requirements. Validated on 416 real-world YARA rules from the Yara-Rules community repository: 82.7% success rate (GPT-4.1, scan-only) and 70.7% fully offline with phi4:14b on a single RTX 3060.

tool_name: Bedrock Keys Security (BKS): Hunting Phantom IAM Users Created by AWS Bedrock API Keys
description:
You create what looks like a simple AWS Bedrock API key. It isn't. These keys differ from standard AWS credentials: bearer tokens that embed the AWS account ID and IAM username in plain base64. Behind every long-term key, AWS silently provisions a full IAM user with admin-level Bedrock access plus IAM, VPC and KMS reconnaissance. These phantom users are never cleaned up, even after the key is deleted or expired, and most teams don't realize they exist. When a key leaks to public GitHub, it powers LLMjacking at up to $18,000/day per region. On its own, the API key only reaches Bedrock, but if an attacker can add an access key to the phantom user, they unlock that reconnaissance to move laterally across the AWS account.


Bedrock Keys Security (BKS) is the first open-source toolkit for the full lifecycle of these keys, across both Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. It scans AWS Organizations for phantom users, ranks them by risk, and removes the ones left behind after a key is deleted or expired. It decodes leaked keys offline, and when one is compromised, reconstructs its CloudTrail activity and revokes it. For prevention and monitoring, it ships Service Control Policies and SIEM detection content (Sigma, CloudTrail Lake, Athena, EventBridge, CloudWatch). BKS turns hours of cross-region investigation into a single command.

tool_name: ICSForge™: OT/ICS Security Coverage Validation Platform
description:
ICSForge™ is an open-source OT/ICS security coverage validation platform designed to help defenders, SOC teams, and OT security engineers validate detection, visibility, and readiness against real-world industrial attack techniques.

ICSForge focuses on what can actually be observed on the network and generates realistic OT traffic and PCAPs (500+ scenarios) in 10 industrial protocols (Modbus/TCP, DNP3, S7comm, IEC-104, OPC UA, EtherNet/IP, BACnet/IP, MQTT, GOOSE, PROFINET DCP) which are aligned with 68 out of 83 unique techniques in MITRE ATT&CK for ICS v18 (82% coverage)- without exploiting real systems or causing unsafe process impact - to help asset owners and defenders assessing the quality of existing security countermeasures such as firewalls, OT NSM sensors and ACLs and identifying hidden gaps.

ICSForge is developed with a safe-by-design approach, operating within a Sender-Receiver architecture and interacting only with the designated sender and receiver, without touching other OT devices.

tool_name: JS-Tap v3: JavaScript Post-Exploitation Moves to the Endpoint
description:
JS-Tap started as a JavaScript XSS and server-side post-exploitation payload with a C2 server. Version 3 moves beyond the web application and to the endpoint with three new implant types targeting browser extensions, Electron desktop apps, and Node.js CLI tools, all integrated into one C2.

Deploy a malicious browser extension to endpoints to steal sessions from every domain the target visits, then inject the original DOM Beacon into specific apps on command for detailed monitoring and manipulation of web applications. Add the optional Sidecar binary to the browser extension installer for file system and shell access through the browser itself.

JS-Tap now includes tooling for patching Electron desktop apps such as Slack, Signal Desktop, VS Code, and 1Password. Get screenshots, keylogging, network interception, and full shell/proxy access (without dropping a separate binary). Custom plugins for common Electron apps allow harvesting of decrypted credentials, reading and spoofing messages, or modifying source code and accessing GitHub accounts.

The V8 Beacon instruments Node.js and Bun CLI tools with a simple environment variable. Intercept network traffic, capture keystrokes, browse files, and execute commands without modification to the target application.

Every endpoint beacon features a browser proxy for live session riding through the target's network. Export stolen sessions as portable JS-Tap Tickets and leverage them with the JS-Tap Conductor, a Firefox extension that imports cookies, headers, storage, and spoofed browser fingerprints. Combine a Session Ticket with a Proxy Ticket to browse as the target, authenticated, from the target's own network by tunneling through their beacon.

tool_name: MachStealer:One Pipeline Behind Every macOS Infostealer
description:
macOS infostealers are the fastest-growing malware category on Apple platforms, with a 400% year-over-year increase in detections. AMOS, Poseidon, Banshee, Cthulhu, and Cuckoo all follow the same credential harvesting pipeline, Keychain extraction, PBKDF2 key derivation, SQLite database copy, and AES decryption. Understanding one family's harvesting stage reveals the mechanics of them all.

MachStealer is an open-source PoC tool for macOS Apple Silicon that reproduces this shared pipeline for security research. It implements the complete Chrome credential extraction chain with parameters matching Chromium's source code exactly.

Feature Overview
- Cookies: session tokens and auth cookies, AES-128-CBC encrypted
- Login Data: saved usernames and passwords, AES-128-CBC encrypted
- Credit Cards: card numbers, expiration dates, and cardholder names, AES-128-CBC encrypted
- History: URLs, titles, and visit frequency, unencrypted
- Extensions: installed extensions with version and store metadata, unencrypted

MachStealer deliberately omits the exfiltration layer: no C2, no network upload, no persistence, no anti-analysis evasion. By isolating the local harvesting stage, the tool serves as a safe, transparent model for defenders to validate EDR detection, develop behavioral signatures, and assess credential exposure risk. MachStealer also enumerates all Chrome profiles on the system with display names and associated email addresses, reproducing the profile iteration behavior of real infostealers.

repo: https://github.com/ultra-supara/MachStealer
