tool_name: Medaudit, an AI assisted Tool for Auditing Hospital Networks and Pentesting Medical Devices
description: Medaudit is an open-source toolkit for auditing medical device network traffic, focusing on the HL7 protocol. It helps security professionals to identify unencrypted transmissions, detect PHI/PII exposure, and evaluate device resilience through fuzz testing and malformed payloads. With AI-assisted triage, medaudit prioritizes high-risk findings, streamlining the auditing process. The tool features a user-friendly web interface for managing projects, visualizing traffic, and exporting results. Designed for network auditors and healthcare security teams, medaudit bridges the gap between compliance and proactive security testing, ensuring safer medical device ecosystems.

tool_name: PETriage: Cross-Platform PE Surface Analysis for Malware Triage
description:
In malware analysis, analysts often need to triage PE files as quickly and safely as possible. Many analysts prefer to keep Linux or macOS as their host OS and confine Windows to a VM to reduce the chance of accidentally detonating malware during routine analysis. In this workflow, however, widely used PE surface-analysis tools such as PEStudio and CFF Explorer remain centered on Windows. As a result, analysts frequently have to boot a Windows VM or switch between multiple tools even when they only need static surface analysis. At the triage stage, the goal is not to execute the sample, but to inspect PE structure, metadata, imports, resources, overlays, and other suspicious indicators quickly enough to decide whether deeper analysis is warranted. Although cross-platform options exist, practical workflows that combine broad PE coverage, CLI automation, interactive inspection, and fully offline operation remain limited.

PETriage was developed to address this gap as a Rust-based, cross-platform PE surface analysis tool. It is designed for static analysis only, runs natively on Linux, macOS, and Windows, and supports fully offline use. PETriage centers on a CLI workflow while also providing optional GUI and TUI interfaces, making it suitable for both ad hoc analysis and pipeline integration. It integrates suspicious API indicators and anomaly detection, presenting triage signals with rule IDs, severity levels, and evidence fields. With structured JSON and NDJSON output, batch processing, and severity-based gating for automation, PETriage combines analysis and workflow capabilities that are often scattered across multiple tools. At Arsenal, I will present PETriage from a malware analyst's perspective, showing how it surfaces suspicious APIs, anomaly signals, and analyst-relevant OPSEC artifacts such as leaked PDB paths, while also supporting JSON/NDJSON-based automation and batch analysis.

tool_name: SafeScribe - Edge Device AI Meeting Notetaker
description: SafeScribe is a privacy-first desk device that generates meeting notes locally, delivering structured notes to user's inbox as a PDF. No subscription, cloud or vendor lock-in. Built for organizations that care about cost and privacy.

tool_name: AC Scanner - QubitAC Automated Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Tool
description:
AC Scanner is a tool to help providers of all kinds ensure their services can resist post-quantum cryptographic attacks including Harvest Now Decrypt Later (HNDL).

The scanner is an open-source pipeline that automates full cryptographic surface discovery across TLS endpoints and SSH services, assessing every asset against NIST post-quantum standards and generating a structured Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM). In a single command (bash scan.sh example.com) it runs subdomain enumeration, DNS resolution, TLS handshake analysis via OpenSSL, SSH auditing via ssh-audit, quantum vulnerability scoring, and CBOM output in JSONL/JSON/Markdown, ready to upload to an interactive dashboard. With NIST finalizing ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) in 2024, and NIST IR 8547 mandating deprecation of quantum-vulnerable algorithms by 2030, AC Scanner gives blue teams a fast, evidence-grade path from cryptographic discovery to compliance reporting.

tool_name: AgentsLeak: Runtime Protection for AI Coding Agents
description: AgentsLeak is an open-source runtime security platform that hooks into AI coding agent engines (Claude Code, Cursor) and enforces security policies before every action. It monitors file access, network connections, process creation, and command execution with real-time blocking, behavioral sequence detection, and a security dashboard. Think endpoint protection, but purpose-built for AI agent sessions.

tool_name: Intercept.js: Context-Aware YARA for Runtime Detection In JavaScript Environments
description:
Many modern attacks unfold inside JavaScript runtimes — browsers, email clients, and Office add-ins — where traditional file-scanning and OS-level controls have limited visibility into application-layer context. In these environments, payloads may exist only as in-memory buffers, fetch responses, or dynamically generated objects. Effective detection requires consideration of not only what bytes exist, but also where they originated and how they are being used.

To address this visibility gap, we present Intercept.js, an open-source detection engine written in vanilla JavaScript that fuses byte-level pattern matching with runtime context inside a unified rule model.

While compatible with standard YARA syntax and modules (PE, ELF, Math, Hash, String, Time), Intercept.js extends detection beyond file scanning. Rules can combine content inspection with contextual metadata such as domain novelty, sender reputation, MIME discrepancies, user gesture state, and runtime origin. Its pluggable module architecture allows developers and security teams to inject custom contextual signals and expose them directly to rule authors, extending YARA from a file signature language into a runtime-aware decision engine.

This enables detections like:
- Executable header from a newly observed domain
- Macro-enabled document from an unknown sender
- Clipboard-inserted script without user interaction
- Binary content with MIME mismatch

Optimized for constrained environments using Aho-Corasick matching, RegExp acceleration, and enforced match caps, Intercept.js runs anywhere JavaScript runs. It enables security teams to shift detection left, disrupting attacker tooling at ingress (T1105), malicious paste events (T1204.004), phishing attachments (T1566.001), and client-side data exfiltration (T1048) — before payloads ever reach disk.

During Arsenal, we will demonstrate real-time clipboard defense by intercepting a ClickFix/FileFix-style attack within a browser extension, showing how content and context are evaluated together to detect malicious in-memory payloads. We will also discuss the engine's open plug-in interface and illustrate how it operates unchanged across webpages and serverless platforms.

tool_name: Keychecker : SSH Key based attack tool for DVCS Systems
description:
KeyChecker is a CLI tool to fingerprint SSH private keys and identify which Git hosting accounts they unlock. In incident response and red team work, finding a private key is common, but scoping impact is slow and manual. KeyChecker automates the two primitives defenders and attackers both use: safe SSH handshakes that can reveal the mapped username, and read only git ls-remote probes that confirm whether a key can access a target repo.

The tool performs local key intelligence first, supporting OpenSSH, PEM, and DER formats, detecting key type (ed25519, rsa, ecdsa, dsa), key size, passphrase protection, fingerprints (SHA256 and MD5), and useful metadata from key comments. It then validates the key across multiple providers including GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Codeberg, Gitea, and Hugging Face, extracting usernames where possible, and optionally using a GitHub token for organization discovery.

KeyChecker also supports repository discovery with a wordlist and configurable concurrency, giving a clear blast radius report like "this key unlocks these private repositories." It is designed for authorized assessments, runs locally, and avoids write operations.

Tool Information
· License : GPL 3.0

· Programming Language used : Python

· Source Code : https://github.com/cyfinoid/keychecker

tool_name: OWASP Faction 2.0
description: OWASP Faction 2.0 is a major update to the open-source penetration testing assessment and reporting platform, and we're releasing it during Black Hat 2026. Rebuilt from the ground up, this release gives security teams complete control over every stage of the assessment lifecycle. We are introducing AI-assisted report writing, a powerful CLI integration framework, a full application inventory and tracking system, and a brand new UI! It eliminates the bottlenecks that slow down manual pen testing engagements and delivers a collaborative, extensible, and fully customizable workflow from scoping to final report delivery. It's built to scale from a solo security consultant to large enterprise security teams.

tool_name: SEmuRAI: Software Emulation and Reversing AI Agent
description: Software Reverse Engineering (SRE) is a difficult and time-consuming task, particularly when carried out on obfuscated or large binaries. In addition, the compilation process also often removes contextual information, further adding to the challenge. Agentic workflows, enabled by the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs), have allowed for the semi-autonomous performance of SRE tasks based on contextual understanding of the problem, received instructions, and interaction with tools. Current approaches rely on static-only analysis, which may not suffice for more complex tasks. In this work, we present SEmuRAI, a dynamic analysis toolkit that enables agents to perform sandboxed binary emulation, complete with breakpoint as well as memory and register read/write functionality. We then conducted benchmark tests between static-only analysis and our combined setup with SEmuRAI across three test cases of varying complexity, evaluating analysis sessions to determine the impact of SEmuRAI on SRE agents. Our results show that the integration of the dynamic analysis toolkit, SEmuRAI, improves the performance of SRE agents, particularly on more complex tasks.

tool_name: Social Engineering with Reel
description: Reel is a workflow-driven, flexible phishing framework supporting credential capture campaigns with optional real-time MFA relay, as well as email sending. All elements are fully configurable via a workflow system, allowing complex campaigns to be developed. A plugin system allows operators to extend Reel's core functionality without requiring code changes.

tool_name: The Metasploit Framework 6.5: Malleable C2 Payloads, New Relay Capability and Protocol Session Upgrades
description:
The Metasploit 6.5 release has focused on expanding evasion techniques in our new Malleable C2 Profiles for HTTP Meterpreter as well as its protocol relaying and protocol session capabilities. This year, we added support for HTTP-to-SMB as well as HTTP-to-LDAP relaying which has enabled us to exploit a number of different attack workflows. We have also added functionality to upgrade different protocol-based sessions to Meterpreter with ease.

This demo will kick off by leveraging the new HTTP-to-SMB relay capability to capture and relay authentication, allowing us to establish an authenticated SMB session on a target domain-joined system. From there, we will highlight Metasploit's new protocol session to Meterpreter upgrade functionality. We will demonstrate how an operator can seamlessly upgrade this underlying, protocol-based SMB session directly into a standard Meterpreter session, bridging the gap between a simple protocol relay and full post-exploitation control.

With an SMB session established, we will pivot to introduce the new Malleable C2 transport architecture, detailing how operators can define custom profiles to manipulate traffic patterns and headers. To put this evasion theory into practice, we will return to our initial SMB session and execute the session upgrade a second time—this time deploying a fully customized Malleable C2 HTTP profile. By inspecting the live network traffic during this second upgrade, we will show the audience exactly how the payload camouflages its communications. The traffic will seamlessly blend with legitimate network baselines, demonstrating how effectively it can bypass modern deep packet inspection (DPI) and egress filtering.

Operating from our new Meterpreter session, the final phase of the demo will initiate an ntlmrelay2self attack from the compromised machine. This stage will showcase our new HTTP-to-LDAP NTLM relaying capability in a real-world scenario. We will demonstrate how we can coerce HTTP authentication from the compromised target host with our low level privilege and relay that NTLM authentication attempt to the domain controller to establish an LDAP session. From there we use preexisting Metasploit functionality to obtain domain admin access with our LDAP session via the Shadow Credentials technique or RBCD.

tool_name: AD Miner – One step further applying graph theory for Active Directory security analysis
description:
Assessing the security posture of Active Directory environments often relies on tools such as PingCastle and BloodHound, which focus on configuration-based risk scoring and visualization of privilege relationships. AD Miner builds on these foundations and pushes the analysis further by leveraging graph theory to transform large datasets into prioritized security insights. By analyzing data extracted from BloodHound's graph database and applying advanced path analysis techniques, the tool provides defenders with a clearer and more operational understanding of how an attacker could realistically compromise their environment.

AD Miner analyzes Active Directory and Entra ID infrastructures to identify weaknesses such as misconfigurations, excessive privileges, and privilege escalation opportunities. Its core innovation lies in the application of weighted path-finding algorithms (Dijkstra) to the Bloodhound graph database to identify the most easily exploitable compromise paths rather than simply the shortest ones. This "smartest path" approach highlights attack paths that represent the most realistic threat from an adversary's perspective and therefore deserve priority remediation.

At the same time, AD Miner maintains a strong focus on operational usability for defenders. The tool provides 65 control points covering configuration weaknesses, privilege exposure, and identity hygiene issues. These indicators allow security teams not only to detect dangerous configurations but also to quantify their security posture and monitor its evolution over time.

An AD Miner report provides both a high-level overview of the security state of the directory and detailed technical insights into the configurations that enable compromise paths. Designed to be used either as a technical appendix during security audits or as part of continuous monitoring activities, AD Miner offers defenders a powerful and practical way to understand, prioritize, and track security risks in complex environments.

tool_name: Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills
description:
AI coding agents from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft support the agentskills.io open standard but ship with zero cybersecurity domain knowledge. This project fills that gap: 734 open-source skills across 37 security subdomains, mapping 127+ MITRE ATT&CK techniques, with tool-specific commands, NIST CSF alignment, and step-by-step procedural workflows backed by 1,000+ runnable Python scripts.

Live demonstration covers four scenarios. First, loading skills into Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Codex CLI and watching each agent perform memory forensics with Volatility3. Second, a side-by-side comparison where the same agent attempts malware triage, threat hunting, and incident response with and without skills. Third, walking the ATT&CK Navigator heatmap showing technique coverage -- strongest in Credential Access (~85%) and Lateral Movement (~80%), with honest gaps in Impact (~40%). Fourth, attendees pick any skill, load it into their preferred agent, and test it live.

Every skill follows agentskills.io progressive disclosure: YAML frontmatter for discovery, structured workflows, and supporting scripts. Apache-2.0 licensed and installable via a single npx command.

Attendees leave with cybersecurity skills loaded into their own AI agent, ready for real security work.

tool_name: EMBA – The product security analysis framework
description:
IoT (Internet of Things), ICS (Industrial Control Systems) and OT (Operational Technology) are the buzzwords for networked devices which our modern society is based on. In this area, the operating systems that are in place are summarized with the term firmware. The devices themselves, also called embedded systems, are essential in the private and industrial environments as well as in the so-called critical infrastructure.
Security testing of these systems is quite complex as the tester must deal with different architectures, optimized operating systems and special protocols. EMBA is an open-source firmware security analyzer with the goal of simplifying and optimizing the complex task of firmware security analysis. EMBA supports the tester with the automated detection of known vulnerabilities on binary level. This goes far beyond the plain CVE detection: With EMBA you always know which public exploits are available for the target firmware. Besides the detection of already known vulnerabilities, EMBA also supports the tester on the next unknown (0-day) vulnerability. There are many other features built into EMBA, such as fully automated firmware extraction, identification of vulnerabilities in scripting languages or hard-coded credentials. To go the extra mile EMBA also has AI integration that supports the tester with the identification of more complex vulnerabilities and better understanding of the discovered vulnerabilities.
EMBA is the open-source firmware scanner, built to make IoT more secure.

tool_name: Ghost in the IDE
description:
The Forgotten Attack Surface: IDE Plugin Ecosystems
Modern software development relies on Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) that have become the crown jewels of enterprise infrastructure. With over 28 million developers worldwide trusting JetBrains IntelliJ, Microsoft VS Code, and Eclipse for daily work, these platforms represent an unprecedented attack surface—one that combines privileged system access, direct exposure to source code and credentials, and a trust model that security teams have largely ignored.

This research introduces GHOST IN THE IDE, the first comprehensive command-and-control (C2) platform demonstrating supply chain attacks across all three major IDE ecosystems simultaneously. Unlike prior research focusing on individual platforms, our framework reveals how a single compromised plugin can pivot across an entire development organization, exfiltrating intellectual property, harvesting AWS credentials from clipboards, and establishing persistent backdoors with the full privileges of developer workstations.

The Perfect Storm: Privilege, Trust, and Scale
IDEs run with unrestricted user privileges, accessing filesystems, networks, and system APIs without sandbox constraints. Developers install plugins from marketplaces with minimal vetting—trusting that "5-star ratings" and "100K downloads" equal security. Our research exposes this fatal assumption: marketplace review processes rely on automated static analysis that cannot detect behavioral threats, and manual reviews rarely occur. A malicious actor needs only upload a plugin mimicking popular functionality (think "AI Code Assistant" or "Git Integration+") to compromise thousands of developers within days.

The impact cascades catastrophically: a single infected developer workstation becomes a beachhead to production infrastructure. Our demonstration shows how keystroke logging captures database passwords, clipboard monitoring harvests AWS access keys as developers copy-paste, and remote code execution capabilities enable lateral movement to CI/CD pipelines and production environments. When multiplied across a development team of 500 engineers, a single malicious plugin represents a supply chain compromise with enterprise-wide consequences.

tool_name: Pentesting made easy - Keeping sessions alive with session-chains
description:
Modern web applications often require pentesters to maintain multiple active sessions across different users, roles, and tenants - a task made painful by shortlived sessions, complex multistep logins, and dynamic MFA tokens. As a result, authenticated automation such as vulnerability scans and exploitation tools frequently breaks, forcing testers into repetitive manual re-authentication and slowing down vulnerability assessments. Existing tools are insufficient for the complex, multi-account environments encountered in real-world penetration tests.

session-chains is our solution to tackle this problem by automatically establishing and refreshing authenticated sessions for any number of accounts. Pentesters define reusable chains that model the application's authentication flow; session-chains then maintains valid sessions in the background and exposes them to downstream tools. Once configured, this allows arbitrary tools to be used without any concern for the authentication mechanism of the target application.

session-chains integrates seamlessly with Burp Suite (including extensions), as well as CLI tools such as sqlmap or nuclei, ensuring stable authenticated testing even in complex environments. As a result, pentesters and security professionals can focus on finding vulnerabilities instead of battling authentication.

tool_name: Praxis - Semantic Command & Control Framework
description: Praxis is an open-source adversarial command and control framework for discovering, controlling, and orchestrating AI computer use agents (CUAs) such as Claude, Codex, Cursor and the like across endpoints. These agents are becoming increasingly prevalent and can read files, execute commands, and interact directly with systems. Praxis functions as a research and experimentation platform to explore what's possible when attackers have legitimate or illegitimate access to endpoints where these agents run. The goal of Praxis is to help us examine and understand the offensive surface introduced by local CUAs and what their behaviors look like for defenders.

tool_name: Surfactant - Modular Framework for File Information Extraction and SBOM Generation
description:
Surfactant is a modular framework for extracting software metadata from filesystems, to help security analysts understand system composition and automatically generate a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM). By analyzing binaries and file artifacts, Surfactant identifies software components, vendors, and third party libraries, and builds relationships between them. The resulting SBOM can be used for system-level vulnerability impact analysis (such as for IoT, Smart Grid, or ICS devices), while also helping analysts prioritize files for deeper manual reverse engineering.

Several major new capabilities will be highlighted in this demonstration. Surfactant can now identify software names and versions by emulating userspace binaries using Qiling, and analyze inter-binary function reachability across an entire filesystem using angr. It also supports automatic conversion of common firmware formats (including Motorola S-record and Intel HEX) to enable scanning of bare-metal firmware for third-party open source libraries.

Additional new features include integration with capa to capture behavioral characteristics of binaries during filesystem scanning, an automated pipeline for generating file content signatures to recognize open-source libraries, and a plugin system that now allows LLM-assisted analysis to surface relevant SBOM insights.

tool_name: Suricata Turbo: Let Your NIC Drop the Flows Suricata Won't Miss
description:
Suricata Turbo adds hardware traffic filtering offload to Suricata, the leading open-source intrusion detection engine (IDS) used by many private and public organizations. When an IDS can't keep up with traffic, it drops packets at random, and threats pass uninspected. Suricata already has a software optimization to drop uninteresting traffic at the start of the processing (e.g., encrypted traffic or elephant flows), but the CPU still handles every packet, even when the decision is to ignore it. Suricata Turbo adds a new offload mechanism and pushes filtering of the benign traffic into the network card itself. Traffic that doesn't need inspection never reaches the CPU, freeing processing power for connections that actually warrant deep inspection. Suricata still tracks offloaded flows through the hardware connection table, so nothing disappears from its view.

Hardware offload supports both preconfigured filtering rules (e.g., to avoid daily inspection of massive volumes of benign backup traffic) and dynamic filtering driven by Suricata's own detection policies at runtime. It works on commodity network cards from multiple vendors with no proprietary software required and is built to drop into existing Suricata deployments. The live demo runs on a server under realistic load, showing the difference between software-only bypass and hardware offload with real-time CPU and flow metrics.

tool_name: Tengu Marauder Vanguard Version 2.0
description:
The Tengu Marauder Vanguard 2.0 is an open-source robotic cybersecurity platform designed for physical red team operations and assessing vulnerabilities in wireless networks. The platform utilizes the Raspberry Pi 5, enabling an operator to deploy and manage units throughout a designated environment from a single interface. This interface, developed on Flask, features a tailored framework. It offers real-time visualization of targets, integrated network scanning, and cohesive management of units.

Version 2.0 introduces significantly more features compared to the original Tengu Marauder. Protocol coverage encompasses Bluetooth scanning and SDR-based RF tools. The integration of an ESP32-C5 module introduces dual-band 2.4/5 GHz WiFi testing, enabling you to evaluate contemporary wireless environments that were once inaccessible. The Hailo AI HAT 2 and Fusion HAT+ work together to bring AI inference directly to the robot, allowing it to analyze targets and make decisions on its own without needing the cloud.

A Banana Pi BPI-R4 operating on OpenWrt manages network coordination among various units. It serves as the primary network controller for the platform, offering access point functionality, traffic routing, and reliable connectivity for all deployed units.

Tengu Marauder Vanguard 2.0 is designed for cyber operators with authorization, wireless security researchers, and individuals who assess physical and RF attack surfaces in corporate and IoT environments.

tool_name: ThreatShield - The Intelligent Way of Threat Modelling
description: ThreatShield is an AI-powered threat modeling and security analysis tool designed to automate and elevate threat modeling using OpenAI's enterprise API. It processes raw documents like PRDs, architecture diagrams, confluence docs, slack threads and meeting transcripts to generate structured STRIDE and PASTA based threat models, attack trees, DREAD scoring, mitigations and ASVS Test Cases.

tool_name: WaffleX: Adaptive Semantic Analysis for WAF Resilience Testing
description: WaffleX is a web defense validation framework for identifying normalization gaps and parser inconsistencies across modern application delivery stacks. Rather than relying on static payload lists, it generates context-aware, semantically equivalent request variants to measure how CDNs, reverse proxies, WAFs, and origin applications interpret the same input differently. By correlating response behavior, enforcement signals, and transformation patterns, WaffleX helps defenders reproduce blind spots, understand brittle rulesets, and harden inspection logic in authorized environments. The framework is designed for large-scale resilience testing across cloud and on-premise deployments, with an emphasis on explainability, reproducibility, and remediation.

tool_name: fetter
description:
Python supply-chain threats, via malicious packages on PyPI or installed from other sources, remain a persistent security risk. While tools exist to limit what packages can be downloaded (JFrog Artifactory, AWS CodeArtifact) and tools exist to scan project requirements for known vulnerabilities (`pip-audit`), neither approach answers a fundamental question: what vulnerable packages are actually on your system?

The recent `spellcheckpy` Python package malware (as reported by Aikido) installs a full-featured remote access trojan: if a developer bypassed package repository controls to install it, and it was not identified in a requirements file, existing tools would miss it entirely.

Fetter solves this by scanning installed packages across all Python virtual environments or an entire system. Unlike `pip-audit` (which only examines requirements and lock files), Fetter finds every installed package (regardless of how it got there) and checks them against the OSV vulnerability database, returning rich vulnerability details and CVSS scores. Fetter can report the highest-risk packages across your entire infrastructure in seconds.

tool_name: MCParasite: Universal MCP Worm Security Testing Framework
description:
MCParasite is an open-source security research framework that brings together a collection of known prompt injection and tool poisoning techniques, and asks a single question: can they be chained into a self-propagating worm inside the MCP?

The answer, it turns out, is yes. What makes the attack surface particularly uncomfortable is how quietly it operates. Tool poisoning happens at connection time, before any user interaction takes place, and requires no exploitable code on the target system. A malicious MCP server simply needs to exist in the agent's context.

MCParasite demonstrates how one compromised server can silently poison an agent's reasoning, spread laterally across organizational boundaries through everyday channels like Slack, Jira, Github, Notion and email, and ultimately achieve remote code execution, credential theft, and backdoor installation without touching victim infrastructure. We tested six frontier models across a range of configurations. Five of them, including GPT-4o, exhibited full or partial worm propagation.

tool_name: Mecha Hayabusa by Yamato Security
description: Mecha Hayabusa is an MCP server that connects the Windows event log analysis tool Hayabusa to large language models, enabling natural-language driven digital forensics and threat hunting over CSV-based Hayabusa timelines. By converting timelines into a local DuckDB database and exposing structured investigation capabilities through the Model Context Protocol, Mecha Hayabusa allows an LLM to execute a full DFIR workflow—from dataset triage and hypothesis development through attack-phase analysis, lateral movement correlation, and structured incident report generation—rather than serving as a simple search interface.

tool_name: PrivacyTrollShield: An Open-Source Scanner for Privacy Compliance
description:
In 2024, plaintiffs' attorneys filed 1,853 wiretapping lawsuits against companies for unauthorized tracking, including session replay tools loading before consent, Meta Pixels capturing form data, and non-functional "Decline" buttons. Each violation carries $5,000–$50,000 liability under CIPA section 631.

PrivacyTrollShield is an open-source scanner that identifies these vulnerabilities in your public facing websites. It launches a headless browser to monitor all network requests before and after consent interactions, comparing actual site behavior against consent banner promises. The tool detects 40+ pre-consent trackers, flags session replay by data sensitivity, identifies form data leaks to third parties, and verifies that declining consent actually works.

tool_name: ReARM: Release Governance Platform
description: ReARM is an abbreviation for "Reliza's Artifact and Release Management". It is a DevSecOps and Supply Chain Security tool and SBOM/xBOM repository & evidence store to organize product releases with their metadata, including various Bills of Materials (SBOMs / xBOMs) and security findings. ReARM maintains security documents and findings per each release.

tool_name: RedTeamSimmer: A Web Based Adversary Emulation Platform and Atomic Red Team Test Orchestration
description: RedTeamSimmer is an open-source, web based adversary emulation platform providing a modern UI for orchestrating Atomic Red Team tests across enterprise Windows environments. Traditional atomic tests execution demands memorizing PowerShell syntax, manually managing prerequisites per endpoint, and collecting scattered results with no centralized visibility. RedTeamSimmer solves this with a Flask server, lightweight Golang agents, and a real-time web interface enabling security teams to execute MITRE ATT&CK mapped techniques in few clicks. Operators deploy agents to multiple endpoints, browse the full ATT&CK catalog, run tests with automatic prerequisite handling, and monitor live color-coded output from a single dashboard. It also ships with adversary emulation plans modeled using Atomic Red Team for real threat actors including APT28, APT41, FIN7, Lazarus Group, and Wizard Spider for multi-stage attack simulations. Detection rule mappings for Sigma, Splunk, and Elastic Security help blue teams identify coverage gaps and validate alerting. A full operations history provides full audit trail for compliance. Designed for red teamers, blue team analysts, purple team exercises, EDR/AV testing, and cyber security training, RedTeamSimmer bridges the gap between powerful atomic tests and true operational efficiency.

tool_name: ROP ROCKET: New ASLR Bypass Mini-Tool & Automating Advanced ROP Attacks
description:
ROP ROCKET is an advanced Windows code-reuse attack framework. This year's Arsenal presentation will focus especially on its new ASLR Bypass Mini-Tool -- this is a major addition that automates building ASLR bypasses for 64-bit Windows. These bypasses can serve to extend pre-existing bypasses. The mini-tool generates nine bypasses for 64-bit high-entropy ASLR, automatically building complete x64 ROP chains that provide bypasses to access to key Windows system DLLs. This approach requires the ability to use ROP, and it can greatly expand the usable gadget surface for exploitation. By gaining access to these Windows DLL bases, the ASLR Bypass Mini-Tool can transform an otherwise limited exploit into one with far more viable ROP options. At Arsenal, we will demonstrate how these bypasses are generated and how this capability fits into larger offensive research workflows.The ASLR Bypass Mini-Tool represents a powerful new capability for 64-bit Windows.

More broadly, the ASLR Bypass Mini-Tool is just one component of ROP ROCKET, which is itself a highly capable ROP automation framework with extensive support for automatic chain generation. ROP ROCKET includes support for direct Windows syscall chains, novel Heaven's Gate transitions between x86 and x64, and "shellcodeless" ROP techniques that can chain multiple APIs together to achieve more complex behavior without relying on traditional payload execution. ROP ROCKET also uses extensive emulation - not only to evaluate individual gadgets, but in some cases to emulate portions of chains recursively - allowing it to solve difficult parameter, pointer, and distance problems that would otherwise make fully automated chain generation extremely impractical. While existing tools only support ROP chains for at most four WinAPIs, we support automation for around 25 malicious, security-relevant WinAPIs.

Another major strength of ROP ROCKET is the flexibility of the chain-building strategies it supports. The framework can work with more conventional PUSHAD-based approaches, but it can also handle more advanced combinations involving MOV dereferences, unusual gadget sequences, while at the same time capably handling bad-byte restrictions and excluded registers, etc. Its internal gadget emulation helps widen the attack surface by making longer or less obvious gadgets usable when shorter, more obvious gadgets are unavailable. ROP ROCKET also includes highly customizable filtering and exclusion options, allowing users to reason about mitigations such as ASLR and CFG, while tailoring results to the constraints of a specific target.

ROP ROCKET helps automate the construction of meaningful ROP attacks on Windows. With the recent addition of the ASLR Bypass Mini-Tool, ROP ROCKET now addresses both the problem of building chains and the equally important problem of regaining access to the code surfaces needed to build them in the first place. For Arsenal attendees, this presentation will showcase both the broader capabilities of ROP ROCKET and the ASLR Bypass Mini-Tool as a particularly timely and high-impact addition to the framework. Recent updates to ROP ROCKET have continued to expand its capabilities, including ongoing support for additional security-relevant WinAPIs and ongoing development of the framework's automation features.

tool_name: Splunk MCP LLM SIEMulator: Open Source AI Security Monitoring Through Model Context Protocol Integration
description:
The Open Soure Splunk MCP LLM SIEMulator is a groundbreaking security monitoring framework that bridges the gap between AI/LLM infrastructure and traditional SIEM platforms. This tool leverages Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) to create real-time security visibility into local LLM deployments, enabling detection of prompt injection attacks, jailbreak attempts, shadow AI usage, and anomalous AI behavior patterns.
As organizations rapidly adopt AI technologies without adequate security controls, this tool addresses the critical need for comprehensive AI security monitoring. By integrating MCP servers with Splunk, security teams can now apply traditional threat hunting methodologies to AI workloads, correlate AI events with broader security telemetry, and detect emerging AI-specific attack vectors.
The SIEMulator demonstrates practical implementation of AI security monitoring through live simulations of common attack scenarios including prompt injection, API reconnaissance, resource exhaustion attacks, and unauthorized model access attempts. Attendees will see real-time detection of these threats using pre-built Splunk detection rules and dashboards.

tool_name: Command Line Threat Analyzer
description:
The Command Line Threat Analyzer (CLTA) is a comprehensive cybersecurity tool designed for detecting and analyzing suspicious command line activities across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The tool addresses a critical challenge in cybersecurity operations: while security solutions often flag individual suspicious commands, cybersecurity analysts need to understand the broader context of attack sequences that unfold across multiple interconnected commands.
CLTA bridges this gap by automatically correlating related commands across time and context, providing behavioral analysis to identify attack patterns, and visualizing command sequences to reveal the complete narrative of multi-command attacks. The tool features over 240 detection rules organized hierarchically by operating system, category, and specific techniques, along with advanced behavioral analysis capabilities that go beyond signature matching to identify novel attack patterns.
Key features include multi-platform threat detection, a hierarchical rule engine with regex-based pattern matching, MITRE ATT&CK framework integration, an interactive visualization dashboard, and an intuitive rule creation wizard. The tool enables analysts to trace the complete story of an attack by analyzing command relationships, behavioral patterns, and temporal sequences across multiple commands, providing a holistic view of potential threats that traditional tools miss when focusing only on individual command detection.
CLTA is particularly valuable for incident response teams, threat hunters, and security operations centers that need to understand complex, multi-stage attacks that require deep command log analysis to comprehend the full scope of security incidents.

tool_name: EMBArk – Firmware Analysis for the Enterprise
description:
Securing products in your environment and across the complete supply chain often means trust in the vendor and its certifications aren't enough. To ensure the security of critical components further in-depth testing is required.
Firmware in this context encompasses the software provided by the vendor of a digital product. May it be a simple IoT gadget or a multi-system factory solution.
EMBArk is a powerful web-based platform that acts as an enterprise interface for automated firmware security analysis. It allows users to upload, analyze, track, and report on firmware vulnerabilities through a centralized system, making complex security data more accessible and actionable. It supports both local (single host) and distributed analysis using worker nodes on multiple hosts.
The web-based user interface, the CLI interface or accessing the environment through an API allows the integration into complex workflows.
You don't have to trust the manufacturer anymore. You can just go check for yourself that the product fulfills your requirements.

tool_name: MORF - Mobile Reconnaissance Framework
description: MORF is an advanced mobile security analysis tool that automatically discovers sensitive information within Android and iOS applications. Designed for security professionals, penetration testers, and developers, MORF provides comprehensive insights into mobile app security posture.

tool_name: Obscurize: Malware for Defense and Counter Offense
description: What if we could use the creativity of threat actors against them? In this case, using a rootkit to develop a security tool which can be used defensively AND offensively. Malware the Securonix Threat Research team has dissected quite commonly enumerates its environment before detonating. It checks BIOS strings, MAC OUI prefixes, RAM amount, running services, and process lists to detect sandboxes and analyst VMs. If a VM is detected, the malware simply exits. STR has build a tool called Obscurize to fight fire with fire. By adapting the userland DLL injection techniques of the r77 rootkit found in OBSCURE#BAT, a publication by our research team, Obscurize deploys 20 Detours API hooks across every running process with zero kernel driver requirement. It has two modes - Defensive and Trap. Defensive mode makes real physical hardware present itself as a virtual machine spoofing checks malware is know to use to evade sandboxes. Trap mode inverts this making a VM appear to be genuine hardware so analysts can ensure their samples pass all their pre-execution checks. The architecture is a Windows Service that reflectively injects agent DLLs into every new process, reads live configuration from the registry, and exposes a named-pipe control interface. Spoofing is applied at the API layer including GetSystemFirmwareTable for raw SMBIOS data, NtQueryValueKey for registry BIOS keys, and stdout interception for systeminfo.exe. This approach ensures consistent results across both legacy Win32 and modern WMI/PowerShell query paths. Obscurize is currently privately published to Github and will be avaialble as an open source tool at the completion of its presentation and demonstration.

tool_name: Pathrunner: An AWS Privilege Escalation Framework
description:
Pathrunner is a new modular AWS privilege escalation tool. Think Metasploit or NetExec, but for AWS and identities. Think PACU, but focused primarily on IAM privilege escalation. Thanks to pathfinding.cloud (created by this tool's author), AWS IAM privilege escalation paths are now more clearly defined and well-documented. But manual exploitation is still tedious. Pathrunner automates the exploitation of all 65+ paths with configurable payloads and options.

Maybe you want to exploit an existing Lambda function and exfiltrate the function's IAM credentials. It can do that! But what if you would rather have the target Lambda function create a new backdoored IAM role for you that you can then assume? It can do that too! The choice is yours. Pathrunner can also import PMapper graphs to identify which paths are exploitable in your target environment, auto-discover destination resources to attack, and chain multiple escalation steps together.

tool_name: Sage: Giving an AI the Keys to Your C2 Framework
description: Sage is an open-source, AI-powered virtual agent for the Mythic C2 framework that uses a multi-agent system to autonomously operate Mythic and its agents running on compromised hosts. Unlike traditional Mythic agents that execute on target systems, Sage runs entirely within its own container on the Mythic server and acts as an AI operator -- it can enumerate callbacks, issue tasks to agents on compromised hosts, interpret results, build payloads, and chain together multi-step offensive operations using natural language. Built on LangGraph with support for multiple LLM providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Ollama, and any OpenAI-compatible API), Sage demonstrates both the potential and the risks of integrating agentic AI into offensive security tooling. The tool is designed for red teamers and tool developers who want to explore how AI agents can interact with C2 frameworks, while also highlighting the very real safety concerns around autonomous offensive operations with no human-in-the-loop controls.

tool_name: AI Attack & Defence Wargame: The Insurance Company Edition
description:
A live, adversarial wargame where every participant controls an AI-powered insurance chatbot built on LLM and tries to break everyone else's.
Each bot ships with a domain-specific knowledge, and sensitive customer data including Tax File Numbers. Your job is to harden your bot against prompt injection, indirect instruction override, and data exfiltration while actively probing rival bots to extract what they're supposed to protect.
This is not a CTF with static flags. The attack surface evolves as defenders patch and attackers adapt. You read your own source code, identify the trust boundary failures, push a fix, and watch whether it holds under live adversarial pressure.

Right at the start, there will be a briefing to show how to play in the wargame. Knowledge of the OpenAI Python SDK helps but is not a requirement. Each player has access to their chatbot source code repository where they can run, test, debug and push their changes.

tool_name: Chef Special: Updates to CSTC - CyberChef-inspired Message Transformator in BurpSuite
description:
Imagine GCHQ's CyberChef integrated in BurpSuite, with live modification of requests at your fingertips. That's exactly what we had in mind when we built the Cyber Security Transformation Chef. CSTC is an extension to the popular BurpSuite Proxy built for experts working with web applications. It enables users to define recipes that are applied to outgoing or incoming HTTP requests/responses automatically. Whatever quirks and specialties an application might challenge you with during an assessment, the CSTC has you covered.
As an example, imagine an API that requires an HMAC appended to all messages derived from datapoints inside the message body. With the CSTC you can extract the necessary datapoints with ease and calculate the HMAC on the fly – automatically for all requests. Together with the CSTCs integration into all major BurpSuite components you can now perform automatic intrusion tests with the Scanner, or manual fuzzing using Intruder and Repeater, without worrying about the HMAC any longer. Another use case is to extract JWTs from incoming HTTP responses and use them in outgoing requests of the Scanner. This eliminates the need to worry about expiring JWTs while scanning.
After our last visit to the Arsenal in 2024 we're back! The CSTC contains new features and improvements, driven by [GM1.1]community feedback, such as many new operations to be used in recipes, enhanced capabilities for sending requests and handling conditionals. In addition, the new CSTC supports multiple active recipes in parallel. Overall, the latest changes make it even simpler to automate application-specific data structures to ensure a maximum focus for pentesters on what's most important: discovering vulnerabilities.

tool_name: Hecate: a trivial UART tool
description:
Hecate (https://tigard-tools/hecate) is an open-source embedded UART implant development framework designed to make common hardware hacking tasks fast, flexible, and achievable with minimal code. It turns any CircuitPython-compatible microcontroller into a powerful, customizable UART implant.

In this hands-on demo, you'll configure a device running Hecate and use it to passively sniff serial communications between two systems. Then, you can extend your device using Hecate, first into a datalogger to capture UART traffic, and then into a payload injector to spoof communications. Finally, you'll see how to implement a full implant-in-the-middle capable of modifying data in transit.

Hecate lowers the barrier to entry for developing embedded implants while remaining flexible enough for advanced research and rapid prototyping. Attendees will leave with a working understanding of UART interception, manipulation, and exploitation, and a framework they can use in their own work.

tool_name: Continuous Threat Modeling in Agentic AI era - tmdd
description: Developers often skip threat modeling because it is manual and disconnected from the codebase. This talk introduces TMDD (Threat Modeling Driven Development), an open-source tool that integrates threat modeling directly into the repository. Using AI agent of choice, TMDD analyzes code to infer components and data flows and generates a version-controlled YAML threat model reviewed through pull requests. Threats and mitigations are linked to specific files, enabling continuous validation as code evolves. The session demonstrates how TMDD can reveal undocumented attack surfaces and logic-level vulnerabilities in real repositories and generate Markdown and HTML reports from the model.

tool_name: GolemHalt: A Deterministic Reference Monitor for AI Coding Agents
description:
As coding agents become more autonomous and deeply integrated into our development environments, they process sensitive data and execute commands with significant privileges. However, mitigating risks like indirect prompt injection, data exfiltration, and destructive actions (the "lethal trifecta") requires more than just system prompts or probabilistic LLM guardrails: it requires hard, deterministic boundaries.

GolemHalt is a reference monitor designed to strictly regulate the behavior of AI coding agents. Utilizing Rust-based hook binaries, the formally verifiable Cedar Policy Language, and YARA-X, this tool intercepts every shell command, file operation, and web request made by popular agents, including Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and VSCode. By mapping coding agent workflows into a standardized Trajectory Event Model, it enforces deterministic policies to prevent irreversible actions, securely manage information flow, and block harmful runtime behaviors before execution.

tool_name: HoneyMCP: A Deception Security Layer for MCP Servers
description: HoneyMCP is an open-source deception security layer for MCP servers that detects AI-agent attacks with one-line integration. It injects deceptive "ghost tools" (dynamic LLM-generated or static) to surface two high-risk behaviors: data exfiltration attempts and indirect prompt injection. When triggered, HoneyMCP produces high-fidelity AttackFingerprint telemetry (session, tool sequence, threat category, context) for investigation and SOC workflows. It supports two response modes: SCANNER for immediate lockout and COGNITIVE for sustained deception using synthetic outputs. At Black Hat Arsenal USA 2026, we'll demonstrate rapid deployment on FastMCP servers, live attack simulation, real-time dashboard visibility, and practical incident response workflows for securing MCP-based agent ecosystems.

tool_name: KEIP: Kernel-Enforced Install-Time Policies
description:
KEIP (Kernel-Enforced Install-Time Policies) is a real-time behavioral security monitor that combats Python software supply chain attacks during their most critical phase: package installation. By leveraging eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) and Linux Security Modules (LSM), KEIP hooks into the Linux kernel to intercept and evaluate network activity from `pip install` and [python](cci:1://file:///home/otsmane/KEIP/src/pth_audit.py:291:0-313:58) processes.

Instead of relying on static analysis or signature databases, which are easily bypassed by runtime obfuscation, KEIP enforces strict behavioral network policies. If a package's installation script attempts anomalous network operations, such as initiating a reverse shell on a non-standard port or scanning multiple IPs for Command & Control (C2) communications, KEIP instantly terminates the entire process group via SIGKILL. Furthermore, KEIP employs a forensic `.pth` auditing capability to detect and neutralize silent persistence mechanisms dropped inside `site-packages` directories. Engineered for DevSecOps, KEIP utilizes Linux file capabilities (CAP_BPF) to ensure automated 100% sudo-less enforcement within CI/CD pipelines.

tool_name: OWASP EKS Goat: Hands-On AWS EKS Security
description:
OWASP EKS Goat is an open source, intentionally vulnerable AWS EKS cluster designed for hands on security testing and learning. It provides a realistic vulnerable environment to explore supply chain vulnerabilities that can lead to the compromise of AWS Cloud resources, including EKS and ECR, through cloud & RBAC misconfigurations.

- Participants can engage in scenarios such as:
- CVE vulnerable supply chain application serving as an AWS entry point.
- Exploiting misconfigured IAM roles and Kubernetes RBAC policies.
- Backdooring AWS ECR images and deploying them within EKS clusters.
- Performing privilege escalation from compromised pods to EC2 nodes.
- Documentation includes implementing EKS security practices and hardening using tools like Kyverno, GuardDuty, and eBPF-based runtime security.

This tool is ideal for security professionals, cloud engineers, and DevOps teams aiming to deepen their understanding of cloud managed Kubernetes security (EKS) in AWS environments.

tool_name: Pentest Copilot V2: The Agentic Pentesting Workspace
description:
Pentest Copilot V2 is a AI-native unified browser based workspace for offensive security. It gives pentesters, red teamers, CTF solvers, and security researchers a single interface to launch and run workflows across reconnaissance, exploitation support, scripting, automation, web testing, and general assessment tasks. Instead of stitching together terminals, browser tabs, notes, proxies, and one-off scripts, users work from one environment designed to make offsec workflows faster, cleaner, and easier to manage.

V2 moves Pentest Copilot from a heavily human-in-the-loop assistant to a far more autonomous system. It can execute multi-step tasks with less operator babysitting, use parallel subagents, integrate with established security tooling, automate browser-driven workflows when useful, and apply guardrails for safer use in authorized environments. It is designed for real security work across pentests, red teaming, labs, and CTFs.

tool_name: TSURUGI LINUX - the sharpest weapon in your DFIR arsenal
description:
Any DFIR analyst knows that everyday in many companies, it doesn't matter the size, it's not easy to perform forensics investigations often due to lack of internal information (like mastery all IT architecture, have the logs or the right one...) and ready to use DFIR tools.

As DFIR professionals we have faced these problems many times and so we decided last year to create something that can help who will need the right tool in the "wrong time" (during a security incident).

And the answer is the Tsurugi Linux project that, of course, can be used also for educational purposes.
A Tsurugi Linux special BLACK HAT EDITION will be released and shared with the participants with also an updated version of BENTO portable toolkit.

tool_name: WebAgentAudit: Security Auditing of Web-Based AI Agents Through Browser Automation
description:
There are many tools available today for auditing AI agents. Yet, all of them require API access to the model under test. In practice, a large and growing number of AI agent deployments are web-only: chatbots, AI-powered assistants, and LLM widgets embedded in websites, often operated by third parties. For these, no API exists. The only interface is a chat widget on a webpage.

WebAgentAudit is an open-source, modular Python framework built to enable efficient security auditing of web-interface agents that cannot be accessed via API. Given a URL with a chat interface, the tool locates the chat elements on the page, builds a communication channel to the agent through browser automation, and runs security probes through it: prompt injection, system prompt extraction, jailbreaks, role confusion, and more. The entire process is algorithmic and does not require any AI/LLM API tokens. When auto-discovery isn't enough, the user can guide the tool with hints or explicit CSS selectors, making it practical against the full diversity of real-world chat widget implementations.

WebAgentAudit is valuable for red teamers probing AI agents during web application engagements, and for organizations auditing third-party chat components embedded on their own sites, where they have no API access to the underlying model.

Built on Playwright, it supports authenticated sessions via browser profiles, handles diverse widget implementations (floating widgets, iframes, lazy-loaded panels), and produces deterministic, reproducible results.

tool_name: Chameleon Forensics (Android): Assume Adversarial Logical Extraction Forensic Tool
description:
Existing Android forensic acquisition tools perform well at gaining access to devices and acquiring forensic data when the device behaves as expected. However, what if the device is intentionally modified to detect and disrupt forensic extraction attempts? Anti-forensic techniques can interfere with commonly implemented acquisition methods such as ADB-based extraction or forensic agent deployment, potentially preventing investigators from successfully collecting forensic data.

This work builds upon the mobile device forensic acquisition process outlined in NIST SP 800-101 Revision 1. Extending this framework, the proposed approach introduces two additional considerations for Android forensic acquisition in potentially adversarial environments. First, it incorporates a pre-acquisition triage step aimed at helping examiners quickly identify suspicious applications on the device that may interfere with forensic acquisition. Second, it proposes that acquisition workflows should be adversarial-aware, designed in a manner to improve the reliability of forensic evidence collection when anti-forensic mechanisms may be present on the device.

The resulting tool introduces an Android logical acquisition tool that assumes the target device may be adversarially modified to disrupt forensic acquisition through known anti-forensic mechanisms. By integrating pre-acquisition triage with adversarial-aware acquisition strategies, Chameleon Forensics aims to support more reliable forensic evidence collection in environments where traditional acquisition assumptions may not hold.

tool_name: MEM-SBOM: Runtime SBOM Generation from Python Process Memory
description: Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) have become an industry standard for defending against software supply chain attacks and supporting vulnerability management programs. However, most currently deployed SBOM tools rely on static metadata such as build manifests and package files to enumerate software components. These approaches are inherently limited for dynamic ecosystems such as Python, where modules can be loaded through conditional imports, lazy loading, custom loaders, and multi-process execution. As a result, the dependencies declared in metadata often differ from what actually executes in production systems. In this Arsenal demo, we will showcase MEM-SBOM, a memory-forensics tool implemented as a suite of plugins for the Volatility 3 memory analysis framework that reconstructs SBOMs directly from the runtime state of Python applications. By analyzing process memory, MEM-SBOM recovers all loaded modules, accurately resolves their package versions, and generates CycloneDX-compliant SBOMs that reflect what was actually running, not just what was declared. Attendees will see MEM-SBOM applied to real-world Python applications, demonstrating how it recovers runtime packages that existing SBOM tools miss and how it constructs dependency graphs directly from memory. MEM-SBOM is designed for incident responders, malware analysts, and security engineers who need to determine what software actually executed on a system, particularly when the system has crashed, been encrypted by ransomware, or is otherwise inaccessible. The tool is fully open source on GitHub, and we welcome feedback and suggestions from the community.

tool_name: RPCExplorer
description:
RPCExplorer is a research toolkit for mapping and probing the Windows RPC attack surface at scale. Windows exposes hundreds of RPC interfaces across core services and third-party software, but the ecosystem for understanding them is still fragmented: tools can list endpoints, yet turning "an interface UUID" into "what it does, how it's protected, and how to test it" typically requires time-consuming reverse engineering and writing custom client code.

RPCExplorer closes that gap by producing a searchable inventory of RPC servers, interfaces, and procedures-and then making that inventory immediately actionable. It enumerates live, registered endpoints via the RPC Endpoint Mapper and captures their bindings (e.g., ncalrpc, named pipes, TCP), while also scanning DLLs on disk to uncover unregistered interfaces. The results are loaded into an interactive web UI built for hunting at scale: users can perform full-text search across discovered metadata (interfaces, procedures, modules, and recovered names) and apply signature and context filters to quickly isolate high-value surfaces-for example, interfaces running as SYSTEM, endpoints with network bindings, interfaces with no security callback, procedures with string or struct parameters, context handles, or methods that avoid impersonation.
For deeper inspection, RPCExplorer enriches interfaces with symbol data where available and surfaces security gatekeepers such as RpcInterfaceSecurityCallback and custom access checks. It can optionally feed discovered procedures and callbacks into a decompiler pipeline (supporting multiple backends) and present recovered pseudocode directly in the UI. Finally, RPCExplorer provides a fast path from discovery to validation: users can invoke RPC methods and run RPC servers testing directly from the toolkit without writing or compiling RPC clients.

RPCExplorer is designed for multiple audiences. Vulnerability researchers can drastically reduce time-to-triage by combining RPC visibility, security-gate discovery, and rapid method invocation in one workflow. Red teamers can quickly profile a target's exposed RPC capabilities and identify promising avenues for exploitation or coercion-style primitives without building bespoke tooling per interface. Blue teamers can use the same visibility and execution features to understand what exists in their environment, validate proofs-of-concept safely in lab conditions, and prioritize hardening around the RPC endpoints that matter most.
Using RPCExplorer, we identified a new UAC bypass along with security feature bypasses affecting the Windows camera and microphone protections, allowing access to these components without user confirmation. These findings emerged while filtering for RPC interfaces hosted in SYSTEM processes and searching procedure metadata for device-related functionality. RPCExplorer's integrated pseudocode view allowed rapid inspection of the relevant handlers and access-control logic, enabling quick validation of the underlying weaknesses.

tool_name: SBoMPlay : SBoM Exploration and Intelligence extraction platform
description:
SBoM Play is a SBoM Exploration and Intelligence extraction platform. SBoM Play exists because "we have SBOMs" does not automatically mean "we can use SBOMs." Most teams either end up with heavy tooling, custom scripts, or workflows that require uploading dependency data somewhere just to explore it. I wanted a tool that makes SBOM exploration fast, local, and practical, so you can answer real questions and move on.


SBoM Play is browser-first and privacy-aware. It runs entirely in the browser, so there is no server-side setup and no backend to maintain. It can import SBoM's or extract SBOMs from GitHub repositories, then enrich what you see using sources like osv.dev, deps.dev, and ecosyste.ms. The main focus is a unified view across repositories and organizations so you can stop treating SBOMs as one-project-at-a-time artifacts.


This session shows SBOM usage beyond vulnerability tracking. We will use SBoM Play to surface tech debt patterns, redundant packages, version drift and sprawl, license posture, SBOM quality gaps, and maintainer risk. The tool is actively developed and the latest features will be demoed live during the talk. SBoM Play was presented at Black Hat Europe 2025, and since then newer releases have added more coverage and depth that will be reflected in this session.
Feature highlights
• Dependency tree up to 10 levels deep (configurable)
• Vulnerabilities mapped to dependencies (OSV)
• Version drift and version sprawl across an org
• License visibility across dependencies
• SBOM quality audit and scoring
• SBOM benchmarking against frameworks like CISA minimum elements, BSI TR-03183, and CERT-In
• End-of-life and end-of-support package visibility
• Dependency confusion indicators
• Aggregated authors and maintainers view to spot single points of failure
• Maintainer funding and sponsorship signals
• Aggregated Insights from all the projects
Reference links
Repo: https://github.com/cyfinoid/sbomplay
Live: https://cyfinoid.github.io/sbomplay/
Tool Information
