• Programming Language used : HTML/JS/CSS

tool_name: SHAREM: Next-Generation Shellcode Analysis Tool
description:
Shellcode remains an extremely important building block of both modern exploitation and malware, yet analyzing it has for too long been far more difficult than it should be. Once injected into memory, shellcode can unpack, decode, resolve APIs dynamically, invoke Windows syscalls, and execute complex logic that often frustrates traditional static analysis. We present SHAREM, an NSA-funded shellcode analysis framework built to close that gap and dramatically improve how analysts reverse, emulate, and understand shellcode.

SHAREM emulates shellcode and can identify more than 45,538 unique WinAPI functions along with 99% of Windows syscalls. For BH Arsenal 2026, we have increased that API coverage by 50%. SHAREM's emulation also supports its own custom disassembler, enabling it to recover function names and parameter information; this information is currently unavailable on all other disassemblers. While existing tools may show only a generic instruction such as "CALL EDX," SHAREM determines and labels the actual API being invoked and its parameters, which can be highly non-trivial with shellcode.

Obfuscation is another major barrier in shellcode analysis. Encoded or self-decoding shellcode often appears as random, seemingly meaningless bytes, leaving analysts with no insight into its true behavior. SHAREM uses emulation to decode and deobfuscate shellcode without requiring live execution, avoiding the tedious and time-consuming effort of dynamic analysis. In 10-30 seconds, SHAREM can analyze a shellcode, presenting the recovered logic with an extreme level of detail--and with an optional labeled disassembly view. Whether the input is raw binary shellcode or ASCII text representing shellcode, SHAREM quickly uncovers the underlying functionality, exposing behavior that would otherwise remain hidden.

Another powerful feature is SHAREM's ability to extend coverage beyond the most obvious execution path. SHAREM can revisit prior execution contexts and explore code that might otherwise go unobserved when shellcode terminates early or diverts control flow. This helps expose additional functionality, including malicious behaviors that might otherwise be missed.

SHAREM also optionally supports AI-assisted post-analysis of its results. This feature iss not part of SHAREM's original, core emulation or disassembly capabilties. It ingests and analyzes artifacts and WinAPIs SHAREM has already recovered, helping analysts go a step further to interpret behavior, identify malicious techniques, and map findings to MITRE ATT&CK framework.

For analysts, malware researchers, red teamers, and reverse engineers, SHAREM turns mysterious shellcode into something that can be quickly triaged and understood, making it a must-see Arsenal presentation.

tool_name: Trajan: Cross-Platform CI/CD Security Scanner
description:
Enterprise CI/CD environments rarely run on a single platform. A Fortune 500 organization might use GitHub Actions for open-source projects, Azure DevOps for internal service deployments, GitLab for containerized workloads, and legacy Jenkins instances alongside all of them. Assessing this attack surface today requires stitching together platform-specific tools, each with its own methodology, output format, and coverage gaps which makes comprehensive CI/CD security assessment slow and inconsistent.

Trajan is an open-source CI/CD security scanner that provides vulnerability detection, attack validation, and infrastructure enumeration across GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps, and Jenkins. Praetorian previously presented Gato (https://github.com/praetorian-inc/gato, Black Hat Arsenal 2024) and Glato (https://github.com/praetorian-inc/glato, Black Hat Arsenal 2025) for GitHub Actions and GitLab CI/CD respectively. Trajan unifies and extends the capabilities of both into a cross-platform framework, while also adding first-class Azure DevOps support and introducing attack support for AI/LLM pipelines, addressing an emerging risk as CI/CD environments increasingly orchestrate model deployments alongside traditional software delivery.

Of these platforms, Azure DevOps remains the most underserved by existing offensive tooling despite its widespread enterprise adoption. The existing open-source ADO tools like ADOKit (X-Force Red) and Nord Stream (Synacktiv) provide API-level reconnaissance and pipeline-based secrets extraction respectively, but neither performs vulnerability detection, targets self-hosted agents, or assesses AI/LLM pipeline risks. Trajan fills these gaps with 6 detection plugins covering 15 vulnerability types (pipeline injection, secrets exposure, service connection abuse, self-hosted agent risk, access control misconfigurations, AI/LLM risks), 9 attack modules that validate exploitability, and 14 enumeration subcommands that map the full attack surface from token permissions to attack path graphs.

tool_name: unrelabel: how to destroy an ML model
description:
Machine learning models trust their training data. That's the whole point. But what happens when someone messes with that data before the model ever sees it?

unrelabel is an interactive toolkit that demonstrates label-poisoning attacks against ML classifiers. You can import a dataset, choose an attack method, and observe how the target model goes from fully accurate to completely useless. The point is to show how little effort it actually takes to compromise an ML pipeline through its training data.

The tool covers several label-poisoning strategies, ranging from brute-force label corruption to stealthy attacks where the labels stay completely clean but the model still breaks. Each one trades off between how much damage it does, how much effort does it take and how hard it is to detect.

unrelabel ships with both a CLI and a web interface. The web UI walks you through a three-step flow: pick your dataset, configure the attack, and see the results with vulnerability scores, confusion matrices, and accuracy breakdowns. It works with sklearn datasets, CSV files, numpy archives, and HuggingFace datasets out of the box.

We also built a companion demo (unrelabel-demo) that puts these attacks into a real-world context: an e-commerce review system where attackers poison a sentiment classifier through fake reviews, vote manipulation, and carefully crafted boundary-sitting text. It shows what these attacks look like in the wild, complete with cost estimates and detection analysis.

This isn't theoretical. If your ML pipeline trains on data that comes from users, crowdsourced annotations, or any untrusted source, these attacks work today. You can use unrelabel to stress-test your own models against data poisoning, or just to understand how these attacks work by running them on example datasets. The best way to learn what breaks a model is to break one.

tool_name: xEndity
description:
IoT devices are embedded in critical infrastructure globally, yet security teams face a fundamental constraint: you cannot aggressively test what you cannot safely replicate. Physical hardware is expensive, limited in supply, and testing against production systems is off-limits. This leaves defenders operating blind against an expanding attack surface of billions of connected devices.

xEndity is an open-source, end-to-end IoT firmware emulation platform that transforms raw firmware binaries into fully functional, network-ready virtual device instances, no physical hardware required. It provides an automated pipeline spanning firmware acquisition, binary analysis, filesystem extraction, emulation packaging, and orchestrated deployment of emulated device networks at scale.

The platform enables two high-impact use cases: first, as a scopeless penetration testing range where red teams and researchers can conduct unrestricted vulnerability validation, exploit development, and attack simulation against realistic IoT environments. Second, as a deceptive defense layer where emulated devices are deployed as high-interaction honeypots to capture adversary tradecraft, collect OS-level and network telemetry, and generate actionable threat intelligence.

xEndity's modular architecture consists of three core components: xQuire (firmware acquisition and indexing), xScout (binary analysis, extraction, and vulnerability scanning), and xFormation (emulation orchestration, network isolation, and telemetry collection). Together, they deliver a fully integrated workflow from raw firmware image to live emulated network, complete with intrusion detection via Suricata IDS and a telemetry sense-making dashboard for behavioral analysis.

Presented at multiple DEFCON events and Milipol TechX Singapore, xEndity bridges a critical gap in the IoT security tooling landscape by making device emulation accessible, scalable, and immediately actionable for both offensive and defensive operations.

tool_name: CLOAK : Cloud Testing Agent Harness
description: CLOAK is an open-source AI red team agent for cloud security assessments, built for enterprise security teams that need AI-driven automation without leaking target infrastructure data through AI provider systems. CLOAK introduces a privacy-first output architecture called Dual Output Rendering that ensures sensitive identifiers like ARNs, account IDs, and resource names never enter the AI's context window. Instead, the AI operates on sanitized operational summaries while complete assessment data stays local and accessible only to the operator. Built as a harness for Claude Code, CLOAK lets operators run cloud security testing directly from their terminal without switching tools or learning new interfaces. It ships with powerful techniques across multiple AWS services, driven entirely through natural language. Operators can issue queries like "check S3 buckets for public access" or "enumerate IAM roles with overly permissive trust policies" and the agent handles technique selection, execution, and analysis. Defense-in-depth hooks enforce dry-run previews, gate sensitive data access behind human approval, and block credential exposure at every layer. A companion web interface provides an intuitive dashboard to browse execution history, inspect full assessment data, and manage active testing sessions. The Arsenal presentation will showcase a significantly expanded technique library alongside AI-assisted technique authoring, where operators describe new assessment goals and the agent generates privacy-compliant implementations on the fly.

tool_name: CrowdSentinel: AI-Orchestrated Threat Hunting Across Unified Security Data Sources
description:
Security Operations Centres drown in alert fatigue whilst adversaries exploit the gaps between siloed security tools. CrowdSentinel solves this by weaponising the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to create an AI-powered threat hunting orchestrator that unifies Elasticsearch, Wireshark, Chainsaw, and 5,049 detection rules into a single intelligent endpoint - queryable through natural language.

Unlike traditional SIEM integrations that require analysts to context-switch between platforms, CrowdSentinel enables conversational threat hunting: "Hunt for lateral movement in the last 24 hours" triggers autonomous execution across EQL sequences, Sigma rules, and PCAP analysis, with automatic IoC correlation through a persistent investigation state.

Three analytical frameworks drive the intelligence layer. Lockheed Martin's Cyber Kill Chain guides hunting across seven attack stages; David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain prioritises IoCs by adversary cost; the Diamond Model maps adversary-infrastructure relationships. All detections receive automatic MITRE ATT&CK technique mapping. When encoded PowerShell appears in Windows Event logs, CrowdSentinel doesn't just alert - it autonomously traces parent processes, hunts for persistence mechanisms, pivots to adjacent Kill Chain stages, and correlates related network beaconing. Indicators discovered in one data source automatically inform queries against all others.

The speed advantage of centralised MCP hunting is transformative: what traditionally takes hours of manual event log tracing, context-switching between tools, and query refinement collapses into minutes or even seconds. A single natural language request can simultaneously search thousands of log entries, correlate network flows, and match against a trove of detection rules - tasks that would consume an analyst's entire shift now complete before they finish their coffee.

Released as open-source software with 79 MCP tools, CrowdSentinel transforms how security teams conduct investigations. This demonstration showcases live threat hunting against real APT datasets, reveals the MCP architecture enabling tool orchestration, and provides attendees with a CI/CD-ready deployment.

tool_name: QuicDraw & QuicDraw-UI: Racing and Fuzzing HTTP/3
description:
QuicDraw(H3) is an open-source security research tool.
It is designed for fuzzing and race‑condition testing of HTTP/3 servers using QUIC.

The tool implements a unique mechanism called "Quic‑Fin‑Sync", enabling high‑speed, single‑packet race‑condition testing (on HTTP/3).
